A Winter Festival Built Around Mulled Wine

On Sunday 9 August 2026, the small town of Despeñaderos, south of the city of Córdoba, stages the fifth edition of its Festival del Vin Brulé. The gathering unfolds at the Centro Cultural “Dr. Juan Carlos Cimadamore” and, as in previous years, admission is free and open to everyone.

The festival has grown into a fixture of the regional winter calendar. It celebrates the Italian heritage of the community through food, music and the hot spiced wine that gives the event its name. Organisers say the aim is to strengthen local tourism and give the area’s small producers a showcase.

For a foreign visitor, the appeal is simple: a single, walkable afternoon that turns a quiet Córdoba town into an open-air Italian street party in the middle of the Southern Hemisphere winter.

What Vin Brulé Actually Is

Vin brulé — known in Spanish as vino caliente, and in English as mulled wine — is a hot drink made from wine simmered with sugar and spices. Local cooks trace the recipe to ancient Rome, where a warm, fortifying cup helped people get through the coldest days.

The preparation is part of the show. Wine is heated with ingredients such as citrus peel, cloves, cinnamon, star anise and sugar, then briefly set alight so the alcohol burns off before it is served steaming. Piedmontese descendants in the area prepare it live for the crowd.

In northern Italy, the drink is a symbol of hospitality, traditionally shared after Christmas Eve mass. That warmth and sense of welcome is exactly what the Despeñaderos festival tries to recreate each August.

A ‘Journey to Italy’ Without Leaving Córdoba

Córdoba province — in central Argentina, not the Spanish city of the same name — received waves of Italian immigrants who settled its towns and valleys. Despeñaderos is one of many communities where that ancestry still shapes surnames, cooking and festivals.

Local outlets have described the event as “a trip to Italy without leaving Córdoba,” a phrase that captures its ambition. Rather than a straightforward wine fair, it is a cultural homage designed to keep immigrant traditions alive for younger generations.

The programme is backed by Italian-community bodies alongside provincial agencies, and past editions have drawn thousands of visitors. That mix of grassroots pride and official support has helped the festival scale up edition after edition.

What’s on the Program

The day leans heavily on food. Recent editions featured masterclasses in Neapolitan pizza, chicken ravioli, focaccia and ancestral crostata, plus stands selling pasta, cured meats, sweets and regional specialities. Live demonstrations let visitors taste and learn at the same time.

Around the gastronomy sit stage shows, ballet and live music, a parade of classic Vespa scooters, an entrepreneurs’ market and a play area for children. A musical bingo has become one of the more popular crowd-pleasers.

The full 2026 line-up is released by organisers in the days before the event, but the structure is well established: a rolling schedule of cooking classes, folk and lyric performances and tastings that runs through the afternoon.

Where Despeñaderos Fits on the Map

Despeñaderos lies in the Santa María department, in the Valle de Paravachasca, a short drive south of the city of Córdoba. That makes it an easy day trip for anyone already based in or visiting Argentina’s second-largest city.

August falls in the depths of the Argentine winter, when the sierras draw visitors looking for crisp air, hearty food and warm drinks. A free festival built around hot wine fits neatly into that seasonal rhythm.

For travellers building a Córdoba itinerary, the festival pairs well with the region’s better-known winter attractions, from colonial towns to the Jesuit estancias that dot the province.

Why It Matters for Visitors and Expats

Free, family-friendly cultural events are among the easiest ways for newcomers to get a feel for local life, and the Vin Brulé festival is a low-commitment entry point. There is no ticket to buy and no camping to plan — just an afternoon in a welcoming town.

It also offers a window into the deep Italian roots of Argentine culture, which shape everything from everyday language to the national love of pasta and wine. Seeing that heritage celebrated in a small town says more than any museum plaque.

Anyone planning to attend should check the municipality’s channels for the final schedule and travel advice, dress for the cold, and arrive hungry. The combination of mulled wine, live cooking and music is best enjoyed slowly.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is the 2026 Vin Brulé festival?

The fifth Festival del Vin Brulé takes place on Sunday 9 August 2026 at the Centro Cultural “Dr. Juan Carlos Cimadamore” in Despeñaderos, in the province of Córdoba, Argentina. Admission is free.

What is vin brulé?

Vin brulé, or vino caliente, is a mulled wine made by simmering wine with sugar and spices such as cloves, cinnamon and citrus, then burning off the alcohol. The recipe is traced to ancient Rome and kept alive by the town’s Italian community.

How much does it cost to attend?

Entry to the festival is free and open to the public. Food, drinks and some activities are sold on site by local vendors and entrepreneurs, but there is no admission charge.

World.title: Free Uruguay Youth Festival Draws Thousands to Punta Del Este
World.content:
Community: Maldonado

Key Facts —Event. The Intendencia de Maldonado has launched Mes de la Juventud (Youth Month) 2026, a department-wide program for teenagers and young adults. —Dates. Activities run from 5 August to 12 September 2026, across the Uruguayan department that includes Punta del Este and San Carlos. —Cost. Every listed activity is free of charge. —Program. The calendar mixes sport, music, urban art, gaming and job-skills workshops, from social football to freestyle-rap battles and a closing rock festival. —Organizer. It is run by the Intendencia’s Directorate of Childhood, Adolescence and Youth, with events centered on Parque La Loma and the Casa de la Cultura.

Maldonado has opened its 2026 Youth Month: a five-week run of free sport, music, gaming and training aimed at young people across the Uruguayan department that includes Punta del Este.

Punta del Este anchors the department of Maldonado, host of the 2026 Youth Month. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Five-Week Program for Young Residents

The government of Maldonado, the Uruguayan department that takes in Punta del Este, San Carlos and Piriápolis, has rolled out its 2026 Mes de la Juventud, or Youth Month. It runs from 5 August to 12 September, stretching the “month” across roughly five weeks.

The program targets teenagers and young adults and is organized by the Intendencia’s Directorate of Childhood, Adolescence and Youth. Its stated goal is to offer sport, culture, art, recreation and training in one coordinated calendar.

Crucially for families, every activity is free. The lineup ranges from social football and esports to freestyle shows, comics conventions and job-skills workshops, most clustered around Parque La Loma and the Casa de la Cultura in the city of Maldonado.

Sport, From Social Football to ‘Phygital’ Matches

Sport opens the program. A social football meetup launches the month on 5 August at the Miniestadio La Loma, framed as a low-pressure gathering for children and teenagers who play recreationally.

On 8 August, the Oficina Joven at Parque La Loma hosts a “Día Gamer,” an interactive video-game showcase with individual and team esports tournaments, a nod to how central gaming has become to youth culture.

A week later, on 15 August, “Phygital Football” blends a traditional match on the grass with digital competition, mixing physical and screen-based play in the same session.

Music and Urban Art on the Calendar

The arts strand runs the length of the program. On 6 August, young artists paint the skate park in San Carlos in an urban-art intervention, turning a sports space into a public canvas.

On 29 August, the Teatro Cantegril hosts “Parate de Rima Deluxe,” an evening of freestyle-rap battles that closes with a live show by artists from the genre, one of the marquee cultural nights of the month.

The program ends on a high on 12 September with “Rock del Este,” a festival of local rock bands on an open-air esplanade at Parque La Loma, paired with a food-and-crafts fair.

Geek Culture, Role-Play and Comics

A run of “geek” events fills out the calendar. On 15 and 16 August, “Punta Anime” takes over the hall of the Casa de la Cultura theater with stands and activities around film, series, comics, video games and board games, according to the Intendencia de Maldonado.

On 30 August, “Forjadores de Leyendas” gathers fans of tabletop role-playing and board games in the same venue, a dedicated space for a hobby that thrives on in-person play.

The comics thread returns on 5 September with “Maldonado Comics,” a convention of comic art and illustration featuring stands, exhibitions and workshops, a recurring fixture of the department’s youth programming.

Workshops Aimed at Jobs and Wellbeing

Beyond entertainment, the month carries a practical layer. On 12 and 13 August, a “McTrabajo” session at the Maldonado campus offers talks on getting hired, aimed at young people interested in work at McDonald’s.

Running through August and September, an online course in artificial intelligence, delivered with the national training agency INEFOP, teaches basic AI concepts and skills, reflecting a wider push to prepare youth for a changing job market.

A parallel initiative, “Ni Silencio Ni Tabú,” developed with the national youth institute INJU, holds sessions on the emotional wellbeing of adolescents and young adults, folding mental health into the program.

What It Signals for Families and Newcomers

For expat families settling around Punta del Este, Youth Month is a useful map of what the department offers young people outside the summer tourist season. The winter timing shows local life carrying on well after the beach crowds leave.

Because the activities are free and spread across several towns, they are easy to sample. Newcomers can use the calendar published by the Intendencia to find events near them, from La Loma in Maldonado to the skate park in San Carlos.

The breadth of the program, spanning sport, tech, mental health and the arts, also hints at how a Uruguayan department invests in its youth, a quality-of-life detail that often matters to families choosing where to live.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Maldonado’s Youth Month 2026?

The Mes de la Juventud 2026 runs from 5 August to 12 September 2026, with activities across the department of Maldonado, Uruguay.

How much do the activities cost?

All listed activities are free of charge. They are organized by the Intendencia de Maldonado’s Directorate of Childhood, Adolescence and Youth.

What kind of events are included?

The program spans sport (social football, esports, “phygital” football), music and urban art (a rap-battle night and a closing rock festival), geek conventions (anime, role-play, comics) and workshops on jobs, artificial intelligence and wellbeing.

World.title: Miró Da Muribeca Honored at Recife’s Free Joyism Day Fest
World.content:
Culture: Recife

Key Facts —Event. Joyism Day (Dia do Alegrismo) is a date on Recife’s official cultural calendar honoring the late poet Miró da Muribeca. —Date. It falls on 6 August, the poet’s birthday; in 2026 he would have turned 66. —Organizer. The Museu de Artes Afro-Brasileiras Rolando Toro (Muafro) leads the programming, backed by federal Lei Paulo Gustavo funds via the Recife City Hall. —Program. Activities typically include poetry recitals, saraus, workshops, storytelling, film screenings and live music, all staged free of charge. —Where. Events center on the Muafro and the wider Recife Antigo district, including the poet’s statue on Avenida Rio Branco.

Each 6 August, Recife pauses to celebrate Joyism Day in memory of Miró da Muribeca, the Black, peripheral poet whose streetwise verse turned the city itself into a stage.

Recife's historic center is the backdrop for Joyism Day each 6 August. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A City Holiday Built Around a Poet

In most cities, a public honor day marks a battle, a saint or a founder. In Recife, one such date belongs to a poet. Joyism Day, known in Portuguese as Dia do Alegrismo, is written into the city’s official calendar of events and falls each year on 6 August.

The date is not random: it is the birthday of Miró da Muribeca, who would have turned 66 in 2026. Rather than a somber memorial, the day is conceived as a celebration, matching the humor and warmth that ran through his work.

The programming spreads across the city with free access, gathering poets, musicians, actors and neighbors around the memory of a writer who made everyday Recife his subject.

Who Miró da Muribeca Was

Born João Flávio Cordeiro da Silva in 1960, Miró took his stage name from the Muribeca neighborhood in Jaboatão dos Guararapes, part of greater Recife. He died in 2022, remembered as one of the most original voices in contemporary Brazilian poetry.

He published 17 books, some translated into other languages, and was known above all as a performer, reciting verse that mixed social criticism, street life, love and faith with sharp, disarming humor. Audiences who saw him rarely forgot the experience.

His standing is now cemented in public space. A statue of Miró stands on Avenida Rio Branco in the Bairro do Recife as part of the city’s Circuito da Poesia, and his work features in the Museu da Língua Portuguesa in São Paulo.

What ‘Alegrismo’ Means

The word “Alegrismo” is coined from “alegria,” the Portuguese for joy, and it is often rendered in English as “Joyism.” It nods to Miró’s own outlook; one of his best-known lines insists that, side effects aside, love is still the best medicine.

Organizers describe the day less as a tribute than as a manifesto, a way to keep alive the spirit of a Black poet from the periphery who made people laugh and think at the same time.

That framing matters in a city where poetry, street culture and Afro-Brazilian heritage overlap. Joyism Day places a peripheral, working-class artist at the very center of Recife’s cultural identity.

How the Celebration Usually Unfolds

Across its editions, the day has followed a full program of free activities: poetry recitals, saraus, writing and storytelling workshops, film screenings, theater and live music, running not only on 6 August but often across the following days. Coverage in Folha de Pernambuco has documented this pattern year after year.

Daytime tends to belong to younger audiences, with workshops and storytelling aimed at students, while evenings shift to screenings, saraus and concerts in cultural venues around the old center.

A recurring highlight is a gathering at the poet’s statue on Avenida Rio Branco, where recitals and performances close the celebration in the open air, in the neighborhood most tied to his image.

The Muafro and the Support Behind It

The programming is led by the Museu de Artes Afro-Brasileiras Rolando Toro, the Muafro, a museum in the Bairro do Recife that has become a hub of the district’s Afro-Brazilian cultural circuit, working with local producers to stage the events.

Funding has come through the federal Lei Paulo Gustavo, a national culture-support law, channeled via the Recife City Hall. That public backing is what allows the day to stay free and open to all.

The partnership signals how Recife values the arts: a municipal holiday, a public museum and federal cultural funds combine to keep a single poet’s legacy in active circulation.

Why It Resonates for Expats in Recife

For newcomers, Joyism Day is a low-cost, high-context window into Recife’s culture. The events are free, centered in the walkable Recife Antigo, and rooted in local life rather than a tourist script.

Even for those still learning Portuguese, the performative, musical side of the day carries much of the meaning, and the setting, the historic port district, is worth the visit on its own.

More than that, the celebration introduces a figure every long-term resident eventually hears about. Understanding Miró da Muribeca is a shortcut to understanding how Recife sees itself.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Joyism Day in Recife?

Joyism Day (Dia do Alegrismo) is held every 6 August, the birthday of poet Miró da Muribeca. It is part of Recife’s official calendar of cultural events.

Who organizes it and how much does it cost?

The Museu de Artes Afro-Brasileiras Rolando Toro (Muafro) leads the programming, supported by federal Lei Paulo Gustavo funds via the Recife City Hall. The activities are free and open to the public.

Who was Miró da Muribeca?

He was a Recife poet (1960–2022), author of 17 books and a celebrated performer of his own verse, honored with a statue on Avenida Rio Branco and a place in the Museu da Língua Portuguesa in São Paulo.

World.title: Bogotá Biennial’s Second Cycle: Five Free Art Exhibitions
World.content:
Art: Bogotá

Key Facts —Event. The second cycle (Ciclo II) of the VIII Bienal de Artes Plásticas y Visuales has opened in Bogotá, run by the Fundación Gilberto Alzate Avendaño (FUGA). —Shows. Five contemporary-art exhibitions make up the cycle, completing the ten projects selected for this edition of the biennial. —Venue. All five are staged in the exhibition halls and auditorium of the Teatro FUGA, at Calle 10 #3-16, in the La Candelaria district. —Dates. Ciclo II runs from 31 July to 5 September 2026, open Tuesday to Saturday, 10:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. —Cost. Admission is free for all visitors, with no ticket required.

Bogotá’s Gilberto Alzate Avendaño Foundation has opened the second cycle of its eighth visual-arts biennial: five free exhibitions in La Candelaria that read the city through territory, memory and heritage.

Bogotá's FUGA stages the biennial's second cycle in the historic La Candelaria district. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

What the Second Cycle Puts on View

The Bienal de Artes Plásticas y Visuales is a recurring showcase of contemporary art run by the city of Bogotá. Its eighth edition is being staged in two cycles, and the second has now opened, gathering five exhibitions under a shared focus on how cities are built, remembered and reshaped over time.

Organizers frame the cycle around territory, collective memory, architecture and urban transformation. Rather than a single subject, the works pose a common question: what holds a city together, and what is lost as it changes.

With this cycle, the biennial completes the ten projects chosen for the current edition, splitting them across two rounds so each group of works has room to breathe in the halls.

Five Exhibitions, One Question About the City

The cycle brings together five shows. “Lo que soporta la montaña” (What the Mountain Holds Up), by Lucas Gallego and Carolina Borrero, and “Fábrica” (Factory), by César Faustino, anchor the group, alongside “SPOLIA,” developed by the collective Studio GL.

Two further projects, “Metrópolis 2027” and “Armas de negación de área” (Area-Denial Weapons), round out the selection. Each proposes its own reading of the contemporary city, using installation, intervention and visual research to connect art, architecture and society.

For a visitor, the payoff is variety within a clear thread. The works move from the physical weight of landscape to the machinery of industry and the layered reuse of old materials, a concept the Latin term “spolia” describes directly.

The curators lean on the idea that urban space is never neutral. Occupation, memory and the ways communities live with their surroundings surface across the five shows, turning the halls into what the foundation calls spaces of dialogue.

Where to Find the Biennial in La Candelaria

All five exhibitions are concentrated in one place: the exhibition halls and auditorium of the Teatro FUGA, at Calle 10 #3-16, in the historic La Candelaria district at the heart of Bogotá.

La Candelaria is the city’s colonial core, a walkable grid of museums, universities and government buildings. Placing the biennial here lets visitors pair it with nearby cultural stops without crossing the city.

The single-venue format is convenient for newcomers. There is no need to map out scattered galleries; the full cycle can be seen in one visit, which suits travelers and residents short on time.

Who Runs It and Why the FUGA Matters

The biennial is produced by the Fundación Gilberto Alzate Avendaño, known as the FUGA, a public cultural institution attached to Bogotá’s district government. It programs exhibitions, concerts and public events from its base in La Candelaria.

As a city entity, the FUGA leans toward free, accessible programming and toward Colombian artists and collectives. The biennial is one of its flagship platforms, giving selected projects a professional exhibition space and a public audience.

That civic backing shapes the tone. The foundation presents the cycle as a tool for understanding social and urban change, positioning art as a way to think through the transformations residents live with every day.

How to Visit, and What It Costs

Admission is free for everyone, with no ticket required. The cycle is open Tuesday through Saturday, from 10:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., according to the Bogotá city government.

The second cycle runs from 31 July to 5 September 2026, so visitors have several weeks to catch all five shows. A weekday morning usually means quieter halls and more time with each work.

Because everything sits inside the Teatro FUGA, planning is simple: arrive during opening hours, and the full route through the exhibitions is available on site.

Why the Biennial Speaks to Expats in Bogotá

For foreign residents, the biennial is an approachable entry into Colombia’s contemporary-art scene. The works are visual and spatial, so language is rarely a barrier, and the themes of memory and city-making translate across cultures.

It also doubles as a guided reason to explore La Candelaria, the district many newcomers visit first. A morning at the FUGA can anchor a wider walk through Bogotá’s historic center.

More broadly, a free, city-run biennial signals how Bogotá treats culture as public infrastructure. For expats weighing the city’s quality of life, that steady stream of accessible art is part of the appeal.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is the second cycle of the Bogotá biennial?

The second cycle (Ciclo II) of the VIII Bienal de Artes Plásticas y Visuales runs from 31 July to 5 September 2026 at the Teatro FUGA, Calle 10 #3-16, in La Candelaria, Bogotá.

How many exhibitions are there and what are they?

There are five: “Lo que soporta la montaña,” “Fábrica,” “SPOLIA,” “Metrópolis 2027” and “Armas de negación de área,” together completing the ten projects of this edition.

How much do tickets cost?

Entry is free for all visitors, with no ticket required. The halls are open Tuesday to Saturday, 10:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

World.title: Brazilian Singer Sérgio Santos Plays Free Fortaleza Show at 70

Music: Fortaleza

Key Facts —Event. Singer, composer and guitarist Sérgio Santos, from Minas Gerais, marks his 70th birthday with a concert in Fortaleza, capital of Ceará. —When and where. The show is on Thursday 13 August 2026 at 8 pm, at the Banco do Nordeste Cultural (Centro Cultural Banco do Nordeste), Rua Conde D’Eu 560, in the city centre. —Admission. Brazilian music master Sérgio Santos celebrates his 70th birthday with a free voice-and-guitar concert in Fortaleza on Thursday 13 August 2026, sharing songs from a new album and a 45-year career with a Ceará audience.

A 70th-birthday concert in Fortaleza

Sérgio Santos, one of Brazilian popular music’s most respected composers and interpreters, turns 70 in 2026, and he is marking the milestone with a concert in Fortaleza. The show doubles as a career celebration, folding in 45 years of work.

It is, notably, his first time performing at the Banco do Nordeste Cultural in the Ceará capital. The choice of an intimate cultural centre, rather than a large arena, fits the reflective, career-spanning nature of the evening.

For a foreign reader, Santos may be an unfamiliar name, but within Brazil he is a heavyweight — a singer, composer, guitarist, arranger and researcher whose songs have been recorded and celebrated across generations.

Who is Sérgio Santos

Born in Minas Gerais, Santos built his reputation as much on his pen as his voice. He is one of the most prolific partners of lyricist Paulo César Pinheiro, and together the pair have written more than 300 songs, including the acclaimed album “Áfrico,” which left a lasting mark on Brazilian music.

His path crystallised early. In 1981 he joined the choir of the “Missa dos Quilombos,” a landmark work performed with Milton Nascimento, and from there committed fully to a life in music.

Across the decades he has moved between samba, Minas Gerais song traditions and sophisticated arrangement, earning a reputation as a musician’s musician — admired by peers as much as by audiences.

The new album “Todo Samba”

The Fortaleza concert arrives as Santos releases “Todo Samba,” an album of previously unreleased songs. It is built around an instrumental partnership with Nailor Azevedo, the celebrated clarinettist and arranger known as Proveta.

The record also gathers longtime collaborators. It features contributions from Francis and Olivia Hime and from Paulo César Pinheiro, underscoring how much of Santos’s work is rooted in decades-long creative friendships.

In 2026 Santos also lent his voice to a tribute album for the late Ceará master Tarcísio Sardinha, singing the samba “No Revés dessa Voz” — a connection that gives his Fortaleza visit added local resonance.

What to expect at the show

The concert is staged in a voice-and-guitar format, stripping the music back to Santos’s singing and his own accompaniment. That intimate setup puts the songwriting front and centre, spanning both the new album and different phases of his career.

He will also welcome guest performers from Ceará’s own music scene, turning the evening into a meeting between a Minas Gerais master and local artists. The result is pitched as a one-off, celebratory encounter rather than a standard tour stop.

Entry is free, with an open age rating, making it an accessible night out for curious newcomers as well as devoted fans.

The venue and Fortaleza’s cultural calendar

The Banco do Nordeste Cultural, also known as the Centro Cultural Banco do Nordeste, sits at Rua Conde D’Eu 560 in Fortaleza’s Centro district. It is one of a network of bank-run cultural centres that host free concerts, theatre and exhibitions across the Northeast.

For expats in Fortaleza, these centres are among the easiest entry points into Brazilian cultural life: central, free and consistently programmed. A concert like this one offers a chance to hear a nationally significant artist without leaving the city centre.

The visit also feeds a busy local calendar. The day after the concert, on 14 August, Santos takes part in an event tied to the new Instituto Tarcísio Sardinha, deepening his ties to Ceará’s music community.

Practical details

The concert takes place on Thursday 13 August 2026 at 8 pm at the Banco do Nordeste Cultural, Rua Conde D’Eu 560, Centro, Fortaleza. Admission is free, and the age rating is open to all.

Because free cultural-centre shows can fill quickly, arriving early is wise. Anyone keen to hear Santos’s new material live will find the intimate room well suited to a voice-and-guitar performance.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is Sérgio Santos’s Fortaleza concert?

The concert is on Thursday 13 August 2026 at 8 pm at the Banco do Nordeste Cultural (Centro Cultural Banco do Nordeste), Rua Conde D’Eu 560, in the Centro district of Fortaleza. Admission is free.

Why is the concert significant?

It celebrates Sérgio Santos’s 70th birthday and 45-year career, and marks his first performance at the venue. He presents his new album “Todo Samba” alongside songs from across his career.

What is the format of the show?

Santos performs solo in a voice-and-guitar format, joined by special guests from Ceará’s music scene, in an intimate cultural-centre setting rather than a large concert hall.

World.title: Galen University, Transparent BPO partner with Corazon Creek Technical High School to expand higher education and employment opportunities
World.content:
Galen University, Transparent BPO partner with Corazon Creek Technical High School to expand higher education and employment opportunities

By Zoila Palma: Representatives from Galen University and Transparent BPO visited Corazon Creek Technical High School (CCTHS) on Monday, August 3, to advance a new initiative aimed at expanding access to higher education and employment opportunities for students in Corazon Creek and neighboring communities.

The partnership will allow the first cohort of Galen University students to begin classes during the upcoming fall semester while working at Transparent BPO, which will operate from the CCTHS campus.

The program is designed to enable students to earn an income, gain valuable professional experience, and pursue their university education at the same time.

Representing Galen University during the visit were Dr. Cynthia Eve Aird, Provost, and Hiram Ochaeta, Director of Digital Strategy and Strategic Management. Transparent BPO was represented by Angie Westby, Human Resources Business Partner, and Abraham Middleton, Vice President of Network Infrastructure.

The initiative reflects a collaborative effort to create new educational and career pathways for young people in southern Belize, helping to reduce barriers to higher education while preparing students for the workforce through practical experience.

Galen University said it looks forward to strengthening its partnership with Corazon Creek Technical High School under the leadership of Board of Management Chairman Justo Veliz Jr., as the institutions work together to provide students with greater opportunities for academic and professional success.

World.title: We bid, we lost: Recinos Group answers procurement questions
World.content:
We bid, we lost: Recinos Group answers procurement questions

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Recinos Group of Companies has issued a public statement addressing what it describes as recent questions concerning its participation in government procurement processes, declaring that its construction arm submitted a proposal in the process at issue, did not win the bid, and was not awarded the contract.

The statement, dated August 3, 2026, responds to public commentary which, according to the group, has referred to a well-known entrepreneur from the Cayo District whose career began in the beauty industry. The group says it considers it important to provide a more complete understanding of the businesses involved and their history.

According to the statement, Maria Estella Recinos has built and expanded a diverse group of businesses over more than three decades, operating across retail trade, construction, importation, exportation, distribution, beauty services, logistics, and entrepreneurship initiatives. The group includes K&M Construction Company Ltd., Salon Essentials Ltd., Maria Estella’s Beauty Salon, and other affiliated enterprises and initiatives, including Women in Business. K&M Construction is described as a Belizean construction company engaged in construction-related works and services, including the execution and support of building and infrastructure projects.

The group states that its businesses have maintained commercial relationships with customers, suppliers, contractors, and institutions in Belize and abroad, including partners in Guatemala, El Salvador, the United States, and Guyana, and that, like many established Belizean companies, members of the group have participated in public procurement processes, supplying goods and services to both public and private sector clients in the ordinary course of business.

On the matter driving the commentary, the statement is direct: “The receipt of an invitation to participate in a procurement process is not, in itself, evidence of wrongdoing, nor does the submission of a proposal guarantee that a contract will ultimately be awarded.” It continues, “In this instance, K&M Construction Company Ltd. submitted a proposal but did not win the bid and was not awarded the contract.”

The statement closes on the principle at the heart of the season’s procurement debates: “The public has every right to expect transparency and accountability, and we support that principle fully. Equally, however, we believe that the public is entitled to receive complete, accurate, and properly contextualized information concerning the work that our businesses have undertaken over many years.”

It should be noted that the statement does not identify the specific procurement process in question or the source of the public commentary it addresses, and no allegation of wrongdoing against the group has been established in any official forum. The statement represents the group’s account of its position.

The exchange lands amid a period of heightened public attention on government procurement across several ministries, a climate in which established businesses and public institutions alike are finding their processes under the microscope, and in which, as this statement illustrates, the right of reply is being exercised as vigorously as the scrutiny itself.

World.title: One month of summer left: Cahal Pech Village Resort is the family’s last hurrah
World.content:
One month of summer left: Cahal Pech Village Resort is the family’s last hurrah

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP):The school year is coming, uniforms are being fitted, and the summer holidays have entered their final stretch. Cahal Pech Village Resort in San Ignacio is making the case that August deserves one proper family escape before the routine returns.

The hilltop resort above San Ignacio is built for exactly that kind of trip. The pools handle the day shift, keeping children happily occupied for hours, while the views across the Cayo countryside handle the parents’ end of the bargain, best enjoyed from the bar with a cold drink as the sun drops. On-site dining means nobody has to cook on holiday, and the thatched cabana setting delivers the away-from-it-all feeling minutes from town.

For families who want one more adventure in the memory bank, the location does the heavy lifting: the ancient Maya site of Cahal Pech sits right beside the resort, with Xunantunich, cave adventures and the San Ignacio market all within easy reach.

Bookings are one call away at 824-3740, on WhatsApp at 671-5737, or online at www.cahalpech.com.

Summer is not over yet. Close it out on the hilltop.

The timing carries urgency. Galen’s admissions window for the September intake closes August 19, with classes beginning September 7, leaving roughly two weeks to apply.
