Poland has urged the European Union to adopt tougher measures in response to the recent migration crisis in Spain’s African exclave of Ceuta, including making migrants who enter the bloc illegally ineligible for obtaining residence rights. During a special meeting of EU interior ministers on Tuesday, Poland shared its own experience of dealing with “weaponised” migration from Belarus, which prompted the Polish government last year to restrict the right to asylum for people who cross irregularly. 🔵 KOMUNIKAT | Polska przedstawiła swoje stanowisko ws. migracji na nadzwyczajnym posiedzeniu Rady JHA w sprawie ostatnich wydarzeń w Ceucie 🇵🇱🇪🇺 Wiceminister spraw wewnętrznych i administracji @MaciekDuszczyk wziął udział w odbywającym się we wtorek (4 sierpnia br.)… pic.twitter.com/glfyiu5ZW3 — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) August 4, 2026 Last week, tens of thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, most of them by swimming there from neighbouring Morocco. Dozens died while trying to cross. Among those who managed to enter Ceuta, Spain says that the vast majority have been returned to Morocco. The incident prompted expressions of concern from many European leaders, including calls to restrict Spain’s participation in the Schengen free movement zone (despite the fact that anyone leaving Ceuta for the European mainland is subject to identity checks). Among those to speak out was Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who on Friday called on Spain to “follow our example if Schengen is to survive”. Poland has tightened asylum laws, border procedures, and has built effective barriers on its border with Belarus, which is the eastern border of the EU. We have invested billions of euros and engaged thousands of soldiers, police officers and border guards. Spain must follow our… — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 31, 2026 That was a reference to Poland’s response to a crisis on its eastern border, where since 2021 Belarus has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross irregularly into the EU. Both Poland and the EU have accused Belarus and its ally Russia of deliberately “weaponising” migration in an attempt to destabilise European societies as part of Moscow and Minsk’s broader “hybrid threats” against the EU. Tusk noted that, in response, Poland has restricted the right to asylum, invested billions in strengthening physical and electronic barriers along the border, and has deployed thousands of soldiers, police officers and border guards there (who have also been given expanded rights to use firearms). A court has ruled that Poland's recently introduced partial suspension of the right to asylum is justified and lawful. It rejected a complaint by a Sudanese man who had been denied the right to claim asylum after crossing irregularly from Belarus https://t.co/jx3s1AxRgG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 10, 2025 On Saturday, Tusk and 21 other EU leaders jointly signed a letter expressing “serious concern” at the situation in Ceuta and warning that the EU “cannot allow uncontrolled mass border crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration, or other hybrid threats to create the impression that illegal entry…is possible”. While they welcomed Spain’s cooperation with Morocco to send most of the migrants back, they also called for an extraordinary meeting of EU interior ministers to “agree on a coordinated European response, including the rapid mobilisation of available EU instruments and the necessary support to Spain”. At that meeting, which took place on Tuesday, Poland’s interior ministry said that it had expressed the view that “illegal entry into the European Union should automatically exclude the possibility of obtaining residence permits, and therefore the possibility of permanent stay in the future”. While Poland’s statement did not mention it directly, earlier this year Spain’s government launched an amnesty that allowed undocumented migrants to apply to legalise their stay in the country. Over one million people had signed up for the scheme by the time it closed at the end of June. In its statement, Poland’s interior ministry warned that “migration must be fully controlled”, as otherwise it can “be used against the values that guide the EU”. It also called for the “official recognition of migration as a challenge directly linked to security”. It added that during Tuesday’s meeting it had “presented its own experiences with border protection in the context of the instrumentalisation and weaponisation of migration and adapting law to migration challenges”, including restrictions on asylum claims. “The example of Ceuta clearly demonstrates that absolute access to asylum is impossible to maintain in the face of such real threats,” wrote the interior ministry, which said that it “welcomed the shared perspective on migration among a growing number of member states”. In a statement of its own, the European Council noted that there had been a “common understanding of the need to continue relentlessly fighting migrant smuggling networks, to reinforce returns, to strengthen EU borders, to build deep partnerships with third countries, and to improve foresight.” It added that member states “were united in expressing strong solidarity with Spain”, appreciated its “swift and effective efforts” to deal with the crisis, and had also expressed their condolences for the people who died while attempting to cross from Morocco to Ceuta. ESPAÑA: CEUTA PIDE CERRAR LA FRONTERA POR LA LLEGADA MASIVA DE MIGRANTES DE MARRUECOS Más de mil jóvenes marroquíes se congregaron en la frontera con Ceuta para intentar ingresar al enclave español, y cientos lograron superar las barreras de protección, que en ese momento no… pic.twitter.com/Mx0LuQwMW2 — Clarín (@clarincom) July 30, 2026 When the migration crisis on its border with Belarus broke out in 2021, Poland recorded almost 40,000 attempted illegal crossings that year. Despite efforts to discourage and prevent crossings, the figures remained high, with just under 30,000 attempted crossings recorded in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have fallen dramatically this year, with only 235 attempted crossings recorded in the first half of 2026. Meanwhile, the estimated number of successful crossings has been falling, from 12,000 in 2023, to 5,000 in 2024, 1,700 in 2025, and zero in the first half of this year, according to the Polish interior ministry. Last August, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked the Polish authorities for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” orchestrated by Belarus and Russia. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Unexploded WWII ordnance discovered under busy Warsaw street
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Part of central Warsaw was shut down today after unexploded ordnance from World War Two was found buried under a major road during construction work. The discovery, which came just days after the city commemorated the anniversary of its wartime uprising against Nazi-German occupation, led to traffic being diverted and residents being warned to stay away from their windows and avoid going outside while bomb disposal experts worked to safely remove the item. W Al. Solidarności znaleziono niewybuch, najprawdopodobniej z czasów II wojny światowej. ℹ️ Czytaj więcej: https://t.co/Fv6oe84XiM pic.twitter.com/BfjQPZveYZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 4, 2026 The object, reportedly around 70 centimetres long, was found early on Tuesday morning on Solidarity Avenue, a major thoroughfare, during modernisation work on tram lines. “We were digging a trench and I literally just touched it with the tip [of my digger],” the operator of the excavator who found it told broadcaster TVN. Staff working at the site were immediately evacuated to a safe distance. Police later confirmed that the item is unexploded ordnance, and that initial findings indicate it dates from World War Two. Bomb disposal experts arrived at the scene in the afternoon. However, they have not confirmed precisely what type of ordnance was discovered or its origin, reports Polsat News. Warsaw was the site of major fighting during World War Two, beginning in 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded and occupied Poland. In 1943, the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, the largest single act of Jewish resistance during the war, took place. On 1 August 1944, the Polish underground Home Army launched the Warsaw Uprising, which was the largest single act of armed resistance anywhere in German-occupied Europe during the war. In response, the Germans destroyed much of the city, around 85% of which lay in ruins by 1945. Warsaw’s historic Old Town was meticulously rebuilt after the war. But many other parts of the city were redeveloped by the newly installed communist authorities, including Solidarity Avenue (which during the communist era was named after Polish-Soviet Red Army General Karol Świerczewski). Thousands of vehicles drove over the unexploded ordnance every day for decades. “Warsaw is marked by history, and there are many such surprises,” Witold Urbanowicz, spokesman for the city’s tram operator, told news website Interia. After the fall of the Warsaw Uprising – which began 80 years ago today – the German occupiers expelled the city's entire population. However, some survivors decided to remain among the ruins. They became known as "Robinson Crusoes" and this is their story https://t.co/UuVbfbcpQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 1, 2024 Unexploded ordnance is regularly found in Poland. In May this year, around 200 anti-personnel mines dating from World War Two were discovered at the construction site of a student dormitory at Kraków’s Jagiellonian University. In October last year, two men were hospitalised after an artillery shell that one of them had brought home from a forest exploded in his apartment while the pair were under the influence of alcohol. Earlier that year, wild boars unearthed 21 mortar shells buried in a forest since the war. In 2023, 72 unexploded artillery shells were discovered during renovation work at a primary school and four pieces of World War Two ordnance were found in the walls of a church undergoing renovation. Wild boars dug up 21 mortar shells from World War Two that had been buried in a Polish forest. The unexploded ordnance has now been safely removed without harm to either the animals or humans https://t.co/W9kaPr1BNw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Russia condemns Poland’s “sacrilegious” demolition of Soviet monument
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Russia has criticised the demolition of a Soviet-era monument in Poland, calling the decision “sacrilegious” and a “flagrant violation” of an agreement between the two countries on respecting places of remembrance. However, Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which financed the demolition, says that the monument was a “Soviet propaganda object” that was removed under a law requiring the “decommunisation” of public spaces. On Friday, around 150 residents in Pyrzyce, a town of 12,000 in northwestern Poland, gathered to watch the demolition of a monument to the Red Army that had stood there for decades. Initially, a memorial had been established in the town alongside a cemetery for Red Army soldiers in the immediate aftermath of World War Two, when the Soviets had driven the Nazi German occupiers out of Poland but then introduced a new communist government of their own. However, the soldiers’ remains were later moved to a military cemetery elsewhere in the region and the monument itself was redesigned and moved to another location within Pyrzyce. Its final form, created in 1984, was a huge rectangular concrete structure weighing several hundred tons and featuring a relief depicting the head of a Soviet soldier. A plaque said “Eternal glory to the fallen heroes 1941-1945” (a timeline that ignores the Soviet invasion and occupation of parts of Poland in 1939). Such Soviet monuments remained in many Polish towns and cities long after the fall of communism in 1989. In 2016, the then-ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government introduced a law requiring local authorities to “decommunise” public spaces by removing objects and names that “propagate communism”. However, only in 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, did the removal of Soviet-era monuments gather pace, with dozens demolished since then. Those efforts were led by the IPN, in particular during the time that the institute was headed by Karol Nawrocki between 2021 and last year, when he was elected president of Poland. Another Soviet memorial has been demolished in Poland – the 43rd since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "We say ‘no’ to Russians who believe these lands somehow belong to their sphere of influence,” declared the Institute of National Remembrance https://t.co/aG9VQVlUQI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 12, 2025 At the start of this year, the local authorities in Pyrzyce began public consultations on removing their Soviet memorial, finding that a majority were in favour of the move, according to the IPN. In February, the town council voted to remove the monument. It will now be replaced with a new one commemorating Polish independence. “We are aware that this change evokes various, often very strong, emotions among residents,” wrote the local authorities on social media. “We respect both the voices of those supporting the actions taken and those who differ in their assessment of the current monument and its place in the history of Pyrzyce.” “We hope that independence – as a paramount value for all Poles – will unite residents beyond differences of opinion and assessment of the past. We want the emerging space to be a space of shared remembrance, reflection, and a dignified celebration of the most important national ceremonies.” The removal of the monument drew condemnation from the Russian embassy in Warsaw, which announced on Monday that it had lodged a formal protest. It called the decision the “latest sacrilegious step by the Polish authorities” and said that it “constitutes a direct and flagrant violation” of a 1994 agreement between Poland and Russia on respect for graves and other places of memory. “The illegal dismantling of monuments is an overt attempt to falsify history, to erase from the consciousness of the Polish nation the memory of the heroism of Soviet soldiers,” added the embassy. ⚡️Komentarz Ambasady Rosji w Polsce 31 lipca 2026 r. w Pyrzycach (województwo zachodniopomorskie) na podstawie decyzji władz polskich został przeprowadzony demontaż pomnika ku czci poległych w latach 1941–1945 bohaterów – żołnierzy radzieckich. ❗️Ten kolejny świętokradczy krok… pic.twitter.com/cKhfFxIL9s — Russian Embassy, PL (@rusemb_pl) August 3, 2026 In response to such complaints from Russia, Poland has regularly pointed out that the 1994 agreement relates to graves and war cemeteries, not separate monuments and symbols, which can be legally removed. The IPN notes that such monuments were “Soviet propaganda objects”, designed to support the Moscow-backed communist regime, rather than genuine places of commemoration. Attending the demolition ceremony in Pyrzyce on Friday, IPN deputy president Karol Polejowski pointed out that the final version of the monument had been established in 1984 shortly after the period of martial law in Poland, when the authorities brutally clamped down on the democratic opposition. “Local communist activists, eager to curry favour with their Soviet masters, erected a monument honouring the Soviet army. This is not a symbol of liberation – it is a symbol of enslavement!” he declared, as the monument was torn down. 💪 Sowiecki obiekt propagandowy zostanie zastąpiony przez Pomnik Niepodległości, a przestrzeń wokół nowego monumentu stanie się godną sceną dla uroczystości patriotycznych. pic.twitter.com/5x4KEzG3Vb — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) July 31, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland’s WIG20 stock market index hits record high
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s blue-chip WIG20 stock market index hit its highest ever level on Monday, surpassing a record that had stood for almost 19 years. The WIG20 has been Europe’s best-performing major blue-chip index so far this year. According to market monitoring website MarketScreener, the index has gained just under 25% since the start of 2026, ahead of the Dutch AEX (16.9%) and Sweden’s OMX Stockholm (14.9%). The WIG20, which tracks the 20 largest and most liquid companies on the Warsaw Stock Exchange (GPW), climbed to 3,963.21 points on Monday, breaking its previous record of 3,940.53 points set in October 2007. It continues a rally that began in October 2022, since when the index has almost tripled in value. “The market continues to be supported by solid economic growth, rising consumer spending, and the prospect of further EU investment,” commented analysts from BNP Paribas, a bank, quoted by business daily Parkiet. “However, after such strong gains, we do not expect the pace of appreciation to remain as high as in recent years,” they added. On Monday, the biggest boosts to the WIG20 index were provided by PGE, Poland’s biggest power producer, and KGHM, a Polish multinational mining company, with their shares rising 3.3% and 1.6%, respectively. The surge was also supported by improving risk appetite across global markets following signs of a de-escalation in tensions in the Middle East. This has pushed WIG20 above the levels last seen 19 years ago, just before the index plunged almost 70% during the 2008 global financial crisis, and then suffered another sell-off during the euro zone debt crisis in 2011. Reform of one of the pillars of Poland’s pension system in 2014, which reduced the role of open pension funds, ushered in years of market stagnation and left the index struggling to meaningfully rebound in the following years. Another decline came during the COVID-19 pandemic and then in the aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. In October 2022, however, the WIG20 started its rebound, rising by 195% since then. More than 30 Polish-listed companies have doubled in value over the past three years, including large-cap stocks such as Orlen, PKO BP, Bank Pekao, KGHM and Tauron, according to an analysis by economic journalist Rafał Hirsch published by news service WNP. Polish state energy firm Orlen has seen its market valuation rise to its highest ever level, and surpass Russia’s Gazprom for the first time https://t.co/w3po4izshJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 12, 2026 BNP Paribas’s analysts, however, note that, “despite a long-term upward trend and reaching record highs”, the Polish stock market “is still valued below many other European markets”. “Our stock market…remains significantly cheaper than the US market and most European markets, but at the same time, when viewed against its own historical performance, it is now relatively highly valued,” they said. Poland’s main stock index, the broader WIG, also closed on Monday at a record high of 148,428 points, having hit several records in recent months. Poland’s benchmark WIG stock index has passed the 100,000-point mark for the first time. Meanwhile, the Warsaw Stock Exchange has been the world’s best performing so far this year "It is a clear signal of the strength of our economy," says the PM's office https://t.co/fIgGWOLLn8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 25, 2025 Analysts warn, however, that unlike in the case of WIG, the WIG20’s record may prove short-lived because the benchmark is a price index, which excludes dividends. When companies in the index pay dividends, their share prices usually fall by about the same amount, which automatically pulls the index down even if nothing has changed in the companies themselves. Monday was the last day investors could buy shares in PKO BP and qualify for this year’s dividend. From Tuesday, the bank’s shares will trade ex-dividend, a move expected to reduce the WIG20 by about 0.8% because of PKO BP’s large weighting in the index. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that the group he leads, Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which is in the process of splitting from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, will soon form a party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes” over abortion or same-sex marriage. However, Morawiecki made clear he retains a hardline position on migration, saying he wants “zero Muslim migrants”, even legal ones, in Europe. He also categorically ruled out ever working with current Prime Minister Donald Tusk, but left the door open to potentially cooperating with the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), which is part of Tusk’s current ruling coalition, and with the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja), an opposition group. Morawiecki u Rymanowskiego: „Do 15 października założymy partię” No coraz ciekawiej 👀 pic.twitter.com/0FrMafvTEl — chrzanik (@chrzanikx) August 3, 2026 Development Plus was founded as an association by Morawiecki, a former PiS prime minister and current deputy leader of the party, in April this year. That immediately prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. Matters came to a head last month, when PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński demanded that all the party’s lawmakers sign a pledge of loyalty and commit to leave any political associations they are part of. Morawiecki and his allies refused to do so, prompting Kaczyński to declare that meant they had effectively resigned from the party. Last week, Development Plus announced it had formed its own separate parliamentary caucus with 40 MPs in the Sejm, the most powerful lower house of parliament. The move immediately made it the third-largest group in the parliament, while also meaning PiS was no longer the biggest. Former Polish PM @MorawieckiM says 41 lawmakers aligned with him will form their own parliamentary caucus, deepening a split in conservative opposition party @pisorgpl. The proposed group would become the third-largest bloc in Poland's Sejmhttps://t.co/coOdpS7pia — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 Most MPs in Development Plus, including Morawiecki himself, are still technically members of PiS, a situation that will only change if they decide to quit the party or if they are thrown out following a disciplinary process that could take weeks to complete. However, on Monday, in a lengthy interview with journalist Bogdan Rymanowski, Morawiecki confirmed that he would establish a new, separate party. That will happen “at the latest on 15 October”, when Development Plus is planning to hold a major convention, he added. Morawiecki claimed that a small group of hardliners, associated in particular with the nationalist Sovereign Poland (Suwerenna Polska) party that was absorbed into PiS in 2024, were “devouring” PiS from the inside, pushing it in a more “radical” direction and seeking to take control of the party and its finances. The former prime minister argued that it had been a “colossal mistake” by PiS to try to compete with two rising far-right groups, Confederation and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), while abandoning the centre ground. He noted that this had coincided with the party’s support in polls falling to below 25%, its lowest level in 14 years and well below the 35% that the party won at the 2023 parliamentary elections, when Morawiecki was prime minister. Morawiecki also traced PiS’s problems back even further, pointing to the decision in 2020 to push for a near-total abortion ban. He claimed that he had, at the time, “warned [Kaczyński] repeatedly…that it would lead to disaster”. Subsequently, PiS fell from support of over 40% in polls to around 30% within a year. Morawiecki told Rymanowski that he and many of his colleagues in Development Plus support a return to the pre-2020 abortion law. “Poland doesn’t need the fervour of ideological disputes” over issues such as abortion and same-sex marriage, especially during a time of “crises, wars and disruptions”, said Morawiecki. “I want us to talk about strengthening the economy, strengthening security, restoring the job market, and how to prevent young people from thinking about leaving Poland again.” Poland’s prime minister has admitted it was a “mistake” for the ruling party to push for the constitutional court to introduce a near-total abortion ban in 2020. He claims “he has always been a supporter” of the abortion law that existed before the ruling https://t.co/QObza3Raxk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 6, 2023 The former prime minister also made clear that his overriding aim is “removing [Tusk] from power and overthrowing the Tuskist system”, which he characterised as a combination of “idleness” and “profound cynicism”, with the lack of any significant reforms disguised by “political marketing”. Asked if he would seek to achieve this by forming a coalition with the far-right Confederation, Morawiecki refused to rule it out, saying that “voters will decide” on the strength of various parties. “But I certainly won’t form any coalition with Tusk,” he clarified. However, Morawiecki suggested he would be willing to work with PSL and its leader, current deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, if they left the coalition with Tusk. PSL is the most conservative part of the current government. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 While Morawiecki generally laid out a vision of a relatively moderate centre-right party that he wants to create, he also made clear that he retains a hardline position on opposing Muslim immigration. “I would say zero Muslim immigrants at all. In Poland, absolutely zero…even into Europe,” he declared. Asked by Rymanowski to clarify if he was talking about only illegal migrants, or legal ones as well, Morawiecki said he was also referring to legal Muslim migrants. “We cannot accept them, because they will destroy our culture,” said Morawiecki. “After what I see Muslims doing in Europe, I don’t want to turn Europe into a Muslim caliphate….The French and Germans…are making a colossal mistake: destroying their own culture, destroying security, and destroying peace.” An Islamic group wants to establish a new prayer centre in Kraków for the growing local Muslim community The idea has drawn concern from some local residents and protests from right-wing groups, who say Poland should avoid "the mistakes of western Europe" https://t.co/ClCwusyhhp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 23, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Pole becomes first person to swim 160km Baltic Sea route between Sweden and Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish swimmer Bartłomiej Kubkowski has become the first person in history to swim across the Baltic Sea between Sweden and Poland, covering a distance of just over 160 kilometres (99 miles). On Sunday evening, an exhausted Kubkowski clambered onto the beach in the town of Dziwnów on Poland’s northern Baltic coast, around 56 hours after he had set off from Kaseberga in Sweden on Friday. The achievement marks a personal triumph for Kubkowski, for whom this was the fifth attempt to complete the route. His effort this year has raised over 715,000 zloty (€166,000) for children’s cancer treatment so far, with donations to his fundraiser still coming in. View this post on Instagram A post shared by PURELY ATHLETICS (@purelyathletics) During the crossing, Kubkowski was unable to sleep and, although a support boat accompanied him and provided food and drink, he was not allowed to touch the vessel itself. His journey of around 160km was not far off the longest-ever continuous, unassisted open-water swim ratified by the Marathon Swimmers Federation, which was the 168.3 km swum by American Sarah Thomas in 2017 in Lake Champlain, between the US states of New York and Vermont. Kubkowski has been attempting to swim the route between Sweden and Poland since 2022, getting progressively closer to achieving the goal. Last year, he came within 11km of the Polish coast before extreme exhaustion and deteriorating weather forced him to give up, reported Eurosport. However, Kubkowski, a former competitive swimmer who now devotes himself to ultraswimming, did last year manage to break the world record for the longest distance swum in a swimming pool over 24 hours, after he managed to cover 103.6 km (64.5 miles). Another Polish swimmer, Karolina Szczepaniak, is also currently attempting to swim from Sweden to Poland along a slightly different route to Kubkowski’s. At the time of writing, she is around 110km into the 172km journey, and has raised almost 400,000 zloty for charity. Szczepaniak, a former Olympic swimmer, also attempted the feat last year, but was forced to give up after 57 hours amid worsening weather. However, the 146.7km she swam set a new record for the longest distance covered by a female swimmer in the Baltic Sea and a Polish record for open-water swimming by a woman. A Canadian multinational operator of convenience stores, Alimentation Couche-Tard, has announced plans to acquire Poland’s Żabka Group, which runs Europe’s largest chain of convenience stores. The company has offered 32 zloty per share, valuing Żabka at 32.6 billion zloty (€7.56 billion). Żabka’s main shareholders have agreed to sell their stakes, with final approval still required from stock market investors. If the transaction is completed, Żabka is likely to be delisted from the Warsaw Stock Exchange just two years after its market debut. Właściciel Circle K chce przejąć 100% Żabki. Cena w wezwaniu ma wynieść 32 zł za akcję =>https://t.co/61XEGuQnnB via @PawelBiedrzycki https://t.co/61XEGuQnnB — Strefa Inwestorów (@strefainw) July 31, 2026 The acquisition will be carried out through Alimentation Couche-Tard’s Polish subsidiary, Circle K, which runs petrol stations, and will cover all of Żabka Group’s more than one million shares. Alimentation Couche-Tard has already secured commitments to acquire at least 57.2% of the company. Heket, an entity linked to CVC Capital Partners owning 37.6% of Żabka’s shares, and PG Investment Company, holding 10%, have agreed to sell their entire stakes. A group of major individual shareholders, together controlling 9.6% of Żabka’s shares, has also agreed to sell its holdings to the Canadian buyer. The investors include members of the company’s management and former executives. They have also agreed to reinvest part of the proceeds from the sale into Alimentation Couche-Tard shares. The tender offer for the remaining shares was announced on Friday by Ipopema Securities, which is acting as the intermediary in the transaction. Alimentation Couche-Tard and Żabka expect subscriptions for the offer to open around 26 August, following a review of the tender document by the Polish Financial Supervision Authority (KNF). The companies foresee the transaction closing by the end of the year. The Canadian company expects Żabka to continue operating independently, under the leadership of its current management team, and to retain its brand. Żabka shares jumped after the announcement, rising from 29.26 zloty to around 31.60 zloty on Friday afternoon, an increase of about 8%. Żabka, which runs Europe’s largest chain of convenience stores, has made its stock market debut in one of Europe’s biggest listings this year. Its IPO was the fourth largest in the history of the Warsaw Stock Exchange and valued the firm at €5 billion https://t.co/fmqLteZjdR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 18, 2024 If completed, the acquisition would be the largest takeover in the history of Alimentation Couche-Tard, which already owns 17,300 stores across 27 countries. Alex Miller, Alimentation Couche-Tard’s CEO, said the company is “committed to supporting the continued growth of the Żabka business while drawing from its strengths in areas such as food, digital engagement, customer loyalty, private brand, supply chain, logistics and innovation”. Żabka made its debut on the Warsaw Stock Exchange in 2024 in one of Europe’s largest initial public offerings that year, with a valuation of around €5 billion. The company is Poland’s largest convenience store operator, with about 13,000 locations nationwide run by around 11,000 franchisees. It has also expanded internationally, opening its first stores in Romania and reaching 100 outlets there last year. Poland’s largest convenience chain, Żabka, has opened the 100th store of its Romanian brand, Froo, one year after launching there. “We are learning from local consumers and laying the groundwork for a long-term presence in Romania,” says Żabka’s VP.https://t.co/0CaZTaVhlB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2025 In mid-July, Japanese retailer Seven & i Holdings, which operates the global 7-Eleven chain among other businesses, also emerged as a potential investor in Żabka. The Japanese business daily Nikkei reported that Seven & i had entered the final stage of investment arrangements with Żabka Group. According to unofficial reports, the Japanese company was considering acquiring several dozen percent of Żabka’s shares from funds and other investors. On 25 July, Seven & i Holdings said it had withdrawn from its investment in Żabka Group but remained interested in business opportunities in Europe. Żabka, which runs Europe’s largest chain of convenience stores, has made its stock market debut in one of Europe’s biggest listings this year. World.title: The split in Poland’s opposition could help them unseat Tusk’s government [Opinion]
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles If Mateusz Morawiecki cuts his final ties with PiS and forms a new party, it may help broaden the opposition’s appeal by offering voters a more moderate, centre-right option. While the strings have not yet been fully cut, Poland’s main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), is splitting in two. A group of 40 MPs led by former Prime Minister (and PiS deputy leader) Mateusz Morawiecki have now formed a separate parliamentary caucus of their own, after last week refusing to sign a pledge of loyalty and quit the association they had formed – as had been demanded by PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński. Former Polish PM @MorawieckiM says 41 lawmakers aligned with him will form their own parliamentary caucus, deepening a split in conservative opposition party @pisorgpl. The proposed group would become the third-largest bloc in Poland's Sejmhttps://t.co/coOdpS7pia — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 The move means that Morawiecki’s caucus, known as Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), is now the third largest in parliament, while PiS, which is down to 147 MPs, has lost its status as the biggest. For now, most of Morawiecki’s followers officially remain members of the PiS party, a situation that will only change if they either resign or are thrown out following a disciplinary process that could take weeks. But unless either or both sides make major concessions, it seems only a matter of time before Development Plus becomes a separate party. A lot of international reporting has suggested that these developments will harm Poland’s right-wing opposition and boost the re-election chances of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s more liberal coalition at next year’s parliamentary elections. In fact, PiS’s split could well help the opposition win a majority. Over the last year, PiS has found itself in an increasingly difficult position. Its support in the polls has fallen below 25%, the party’s lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, combined support for two far-right opposition groups – Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) – has risen to over 20%, threatening PiS’s longstanding dominance on the right. In response, Kaczyński has pushed his party in a more rightward direction, picking a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s prime ministerial candidate in March. That signalled that PiS was aiming to compete head to head with the far right on many issues, taking tougher positions on Ukraine, the EU, migration and climate policy. In many cases, that meant disowning the legacy of the PiS government led by Morawiecki from 2017 to 2023. It also meant that the party was ceding the centre ground, something Morawiecki, who represents the more moderate, technocratic side of PiS, was particularly concerned about (alongside his own waning influence). When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal. This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 Should Morawiecki now, as expected, launch his own centre-right party, focused on economic development, it would appeal to moderate conservatives who are opposed to the Tusk government but put off by the far right and PiS’s own hardline turn. Inevitably, some of the support for Development Plus would come at the expense of PiS – but not all of it, and possibly not even most of it. An example of something similar happening can be seen elsewhere among the opposition. Until last year, KKP was part of Confederation. However, its leader, Grzegorz Braun, was expelled after announcing a run for the presidency against Confederation’s official candidate, Sławomir Mentzen. In June 2025, KKP formed its own parliamentary caucus. Since then, support for Confederation has remained stable at around 13-14%, while KKP has risen to over 9% in the polls. So, by splitting, the two groups actually increased the size of their potential electorate, with KKP successfully appealing to an even more radical pool of voters than Confederation. It is possible that Morawiecki could do the same in the opposite direction – his new party winning over moderate conservatives while PiS continues to appeal to its most loyal supporters as well as competing with the far right. There certainly seems to be fertile ground for such a party. Regular polling by the state research agency CBOS shows that the proportion of Poles with a negative view of Tusk’s government rose to its joint-highest level this month, at 48%, while only 29% have a positive view. The last time that positive views outnumbered negative ones was in February 2024, the second full month of the current ruling coalition’s time in power. Among those who voted for Tusk and his allies in 2023, dissatisfaction is strongest among moderate conservatives. Both Tusk’s centrist KO and one of his coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), are polling only slightly below the proportion of votes they received in that year (30.7% and 8.6%, respectively). However, the most conservative part of the coalition, the centre-right Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance, has fallen from 14.4% of the vote in 2023 to only around 4-5% today for the two parties that constituted it, Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) and the Polish People’s Party (PSL) (which last year decided to go their separate ways). An IBRiS poll for Polsat News in April this year found that, whereas 84% of KO voters and 57.1% of Left voters have a positive view of Tusk’s government, that figure falls to 42.5% for Third Way voters, a majority of whom (51.6%) have a negative opinion. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 Moderate conservatives’ disillusionment with the government, combined with PiS’s shift away from the centre ground, gives a clear opportunity for Morawiecki. And Tusk’s coalition itself showed in 2023 the advantages for the opposition in offering a broader set of options. While some – in KO in particular – had pushed for centrist and left-wing parties to stand jointly on a single list at that year’s elections, instead they campaigned as three main blocs. That gave voters opposed to the PiS government a genuine choice, and likely played a big part in the record turnout that helped bring Tusk’s coalition to power. It is similarly possible now that a four-branched opposition, ranging from Morawiecki on the centre right, through PiS and Confederation, to Braun on the radical right, could together win a parliamentary majority. Polls currently show those four groups with combined support of around 50% (though polling regarding support for Morawiecki’s prospective party should for now be treated with caution). Jestem dumny z tego, co wspólnie zrobiliśmy dla Polski. I wiem jedno – nasza misja wciąż trwa💪🇵🇱#RozwojPlus pic.twitter.com/xOnxKDoroS — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 31, 2026 However, even if they do win a majority, it is far from certain what would happen then. In 2023, the three opposition blocs were, although standing separately, clearly aligned with one another and focused on removing PiS from power. When they together won a parliamentary majority, it was absolutely clear they would form a coalition government. By contrast, today’s opposition is deeply divided. Confederation and KKP regularly attack PiS. It is not at all clear that Confederation would be willing to form a coalition government with PiS, while Kaczyński has explicitly ruled out working with the pro-Russian, anti-American Braun. Meanwhile, Morawiecki’s split has followed months of bitter infighting within PiS, which has often been carried out in public. The manner in which he and his allies are now departing the party means that relations with PiS are likely to remain difficult. The national-conservative opposition PiS party's newly named candidate for prime minister has made overtures to the far-right Confederation. But he also ruled out Grzegorz Braun, an even more radical far-right figure, serving in a PiS-led government https://t.co/i3zOZJWdUN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 9, 2026 It would therefore be hard for the opposition to form a government, even if they do win a majority. In this situation, the role of President Karol Nawrocki may be vital. Though elected with the support of PiS last year, he was technically an independent and maintained good relations with Confederation and even, to some extent, Braun (who endorsed Nawrocki after being eliminated in the first round). When Morawiecki this week announced the “ten pillars” of Development Plus’s programme, he made clear his loyalty to Nawrocki: the second of those pillars is “respect for the president”. Nie ma silnej Polski bez wielkich ambicji. Nie ma wielkich ambicji bez ludzi, którzy je zdefiniują i będą gotowi wziąć odpowiedzialność za ich realizację. Bezpieczeństwo. Rozwój. Suwerenność. Ambicja. Tożsamość. Patriotyzm. To nie hasła wyborcze, ale fundamenty państwa, które… pic.twitter.com/G0YBbfhLye — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 28, 2026 Many on the right hope that Nawrocki can play a role next year in helping the opposition present a more united front during the election campaign. It is also the president who decides who gets the opportunity to try to form a government after the elections. That role would be of particular significance if, as is very possible, Tusk’s KO emerges as the biggest individual party but the opposition together may be able to form a parliamentary majority. Given that we are still over 14 months away from the elections, and Morawiecki has not even yet officially split from PiS, it is still far too early to make confident predictions. However, while Morawiecki’s likely departure is clearly a personal blow to Kaczyński – and a sign of the 77-year-old’s waning influence over not only the Polish right but even his own party – it may conversely provide a boost to the opposition as a whole. World.title: GALLERY: Time Capsule Buried Beneath Prague’s Wenceslas Square Tramline
World.content:
A time capsule containing different items, newspapers and messages documenting life in 2026 has been buried beneath Prague’s reconstructed Wenceslas Square.

The capsule was placed on Wednesday, August 5, near the statue of St. Wenceslas as work continues on the upper section of the square.

The Prague New Town Association, which is involved in activities around the statue and the surrounding area, organised the ceremony.

The date was not originally chosen for its historical significance. Construction work ultimately determined both the day and the location of the burial. But the association later discovered that August 5 also marks the 60th anniversary of the release of the Beatles’ Revolver album.

“We were wondering what made August 5 go down in history. Then we found out that it was 60 years ago that the Beatles released their famous album Revolver. So now we are leaving a message here for future generations,” said Monika Vlková, the association’s executive director.



The box, measuring 60 by 40 by 23.5 centimetres and weighing about eight kilograms, was then taken to a prepared pit beside the statue. Workers had excavated the hole to a depth of around 1.7 metres, where the capsule was placed before the site was covered.

The container had been wrapped in transparent protective film, as had its contents.

The collection includes coins, newspapers published during the first week of August 2026, T-shirts, badges and written messages. It also contains proposals submitted by architects during the competition for the redesign of Wenceslas Square.

The box reportedly also holds a hammer and a beer glass.

The objects are accompanied by a 20-page report describing everyday life in the Czech capital in 2026. The capsule also contains USB drives with digital material documenting the period of the Covid-19 pandemic and its effects on life in central Prague.

The capsule is intended to remain underground for decades. The association estimates that Wenceslas Square could undergo another major reconstruction in roughly 50 years, although nobody can predict when the next intervention will actually take place.

World.title: Czechia Tightens Temporary Protection Rules for Ukrainian Men Aged 23 to 60
World.content:
New rules affecting Ukrainian men seeking temporary protection in the Czech Republic will take effect on August 5, 2026.

Under the changes, men aged 23 to 60 applying for temporary protection will have to demonstrate that they are exempt from military service in Ukraine.

The requirement will apply to new applications and certain other applications for protection, but not to people who already hold valid temporary protection.



The Czech Interior Ministry says the new rules follow an EU Council decision published in the Official Journal of the European Union on August 4. The decision also extends temporary protection for people fleeing Russia’s war in Ukraine until March 31, 2028.

For applicants aged 23 to 60, military registration documents will be checked as part of the application process. Applicants will use Ukraine’s Reserv+ system to demonstrate their military status, with the electronic military registration document showing whether they are exempt from military service.

The rules are different for younger applicants. People aged 18 to 22 will only need to demonstrate that they are registered in the Reserv+ system.

The new requirement concerns people applying for temporary protection for the first time, as well as repeat applications and applications connected with family reunification. It does not apply to people who already have valid temporary protection.

The military-service requirement will also not be introduced as part of the regular extension process. Ukrainians whose temporary protection is already valid will therefore not have to provide this additional documentation when extending their status through March 2028.

Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar said the Czech government had pushed for stricter conditions for new applicants. According to the ministry, the change is expected to reduce the number of new arrivals and ease pressure on public services, including health care and social security.

World.title: Filming of American Spy Series to Bring Restrictions to Prague 7
World.content:
Filming for the American series Birdwatcher will take place at the Prague 7 tax office on Kapitána Jaroše Embankment from August 8 to 24, bringing temporary restrictions to the area.

The production will use the tax office building at Kapitána Jaroše Embankment 1000/7, while part of the sidewalk outside the building will be closed to accommodate filming equipment.

The restrictions will not affect the normal operation of the tax office.



Drivers should also expect temporary parking restrictions on nearby Na Ovčinách Street. Vehicles will still be allowed to pass through the street, but parking will be prohibited during the designated filming periods.

The restrictions will not be in force continuously throughout the filming period. They will apply only on specific dates, with Prague 7 publishing a map showing the affected areas and individual dates on its website.

Prague has become a major filming location

Birdwatcher is an American spy fantasy series set during the Cold War. The production is being led by Legendary and Apple TV, with Andy Goddard directing. Wyatt Russell plays the lead role.

The story follows Colonel Lee Shaw as he embarks on a covert mission behind enemy lines to prevent the Soviet Union from unleashing a new Titan capable of devastating the United States and altering the balance of the Cold War.

The series is set in the 20th century against the backdrop of the Cold War, and parts of the production are being filmed in Prague.

Czech production company Stillking Films is handling the local production. The company has previously worked on major international productions filmed in the Czech capital, including The Gray Man.

World.title: Seven Prague Rooftops to Visit Before Summer Ends
World.content:
Summer is already moving on, and Prague’s rooftop season won’t last much longer.

August is the time to make the most of the city’s terraces, sunset views and outdoor events before they disappear for another year.

Here are seven rooftops and terraces worth visiting before autumn arrives.



1. REASON at Masaryčka

Eleven floors above Masaryk Station, REASON offers one of Prague’s newest rooftop dining spots, with views over the city and the Zaha Hadid-designed Masaryčka development.

This summer, its terrace is also home to the seasonal Frerejean Frères Champagne Bar, serving champagne by the glass, cocktails, oysters and light bites. The menu includes THE REASON KIR, made with herbs grown on the rooftop.

This summer: Champagne, oysters and cocktails above Masaryčka.

2. W Prague – ABOVE Rooftop

ABOVE Rooftop at W Prague brings a Mediterranean feel to the top of Wenceslas Square.

The daily Mediterranean Hour runs from 5 to 6 PM, with two spritzes and a Taste of the Mediterranean platter for CZK 990. Oysters are also served from Thursday to Saturday, alongside a programme of summer events and pop-ups.

This summer: Mediterranean Hour, sunset drinks and oysters in the centre.

3. MINUTY Rooftop Terrace

The rooftop at Fairmont Golden Prague offers views across Pařížská, Letná and the city centre from nine floors up.

MINUTY Rooftop Terrace by Golden Eye focuses on champagne, oysters, caviar and cocktails. The terrace is seasonal and is expected to remain open until September, weather permitting.

This summer: Champagne, oysters and caviar with a view.

4. Sky Lounge 360°

For the view alone, Sky Lounge 360° is hard to beat. The rooftop looks across Prague’s historic centre and becomes livelier during the summer months, with DJs, sunset events and Prague Rooftop Festival activities.

It is more about drinks and atmosphere than a long dinner — a good option for an evening that starts at sunset and continues after dark.

This summer: Sunset events, DJs and panoramic views.

5. The Cloud One Rooftop

The Cloud One Prague on Hybernská has its own rooftop cocktail bar overlooking the Masaryčka area.

The relaxed terrace works well for an after-work drink, while summer events bring DJs and a livelier atmosphere at sunset. It has also joined the Prague Rooftop Festival programme.

And if you want to make a night of it, REASON is just a short walk away.

This summer: Cocktails, sunset events and views of Masaryčka.

6. Casablanca Sky Bar

On the sixth floor of The President Hotel, Casablanca Sky Bar looks out over the Vltava and Prague skyline.

With DJs, cocktails and regular sunset events, it has more of a party atmosphere than a traditional hotel rooftop. It is also one of the venues taking part in the Prague Rooftop Festival.

This summer: DJs, cocktails and sunset parties above the Vltava.

7. Monkey Bar

Monkey Bar at Falkensteiner Hotel Prague is a quieter alternative, with a green, jungle-style terrace close to the main railway station.

Every Thursday until the end of August, the terrace hosts BBQ & Beats, combining barbecue, live music and summer drinks. Frozen margaritas are also on the menu.

For daytime plans, there is Jungle Brunch, including a bottomless mimosa option.

This summer: BBQ & Beats every Thursday through August.

World.title: Prague Kettlebell Brand Železná Koule Opens 600-Square-Metre Gym in Karlín
World.content:
Czech kettlebell training brand Železná Koule has opened its largest location yet at Danube House in Prague’s Karlín district.

The new 600-square-metre gym expands the brand’s presence in Prague and comes ahead of the next edition of its flagship Amazing 12 fitness programme.

Železná Koule has built a community around kettlebell training and coached workouts rather than the traditional self-service gym model. The company says more than 20,000 people have trained through its programmes since its launch.

At its Karlín location, members train under the guidance of coaches in small groups. The approach is designed to provide more personal instruction and a structured training environment, rather than simply giving members access to gym equipment.



The new location is also the latest venue for the company’s Amazing 12 programme, a 12-week fitness and body transformation course that combines regular training with nutrition guidance and ongoing support.

What is the Amazing 12 programme?

The programme is aimed at both people who are new to structured strength training and more experienced gym-goers looking for a more organised approach to their workouts.

Although the programme itself lasts 12 weeks, participants first complete a preparation week, making 13 weeks in total. During the programme, they take part in 64 training sessions, with one-hour workouts held every weekday under the supervision of a coach.

Groups are limited to a maximum of five participants, allowing coaches to work closely with each person throughout the programme.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Železná koule (@zelezna_koule)

The programme is designed to provide a structured routine covering exercise, nutrition and recovery, with progress tracked throughout the 12 weeks.

The next Amazing 12 programme starts on August 31, 2026, with places available at the new Karlín location as well as Železná Koule gyms in Smíchov and Strašnice.

The Karlín opening is part of the continued expansion of a Czech fitness brand that has developed a following around kettlebell-based training and small-group coaching. For people unfamiliar with the name, Železná Koule roughly translates from Czech as “iron ball,” referring to the kettlebell at the centre of its training approach.

More information about the Amazing 12 programme, including registration, is available at amazing12.cz.

World.title: A New Bus Line to Prague Airport Could Launch This Autumn
World.content:
A new private bus service could soon connect Prague’s main railway station directly with Václav Havel Airport, offering passengers another option for getting between the city center and the airport.

Transport company Dinarica is planning to launch the service at the end of October. The route would run between the main railway station and the airport, providing a direct alternative to the Airport Express operated by České dráhy.

The company says it wants to address one of the main practical problems passengers face when travelling by bus to the airport — luggage storage.

Dinarica plans to use Setra and MAN buses equipped with air conditioning, seat belts and more spacious seating. Each vehicle will accommodate between 70 and 90 passengers.



The planned service would operate from morning until evening, with buses running approximately every two hours.

A one-way ticket is expected to cost around CZK 125, making the service considerably cheaper than the Airport Express. Its fare is set to rise to CZK 200 following the latest price increase.

Prague’s public transport system already offers cheaper ways to reach the airport. Trolleybus 59 and bus 100 connect Václav Havel Airport with the Prague public transport network, but neither provides a direct connection to the main railway station.

Both services are primarily designed as part of the regular city transport system.

If approved and launched as planned, the Dinarica service would give passengers another direct option between Prague’s main railway station and the airport, with a lower fare than the Airport Express.

World.title: More Than Half of Czech Households Could Be Overpaying for Electricity
World.content:
A large number of Czech households may be paying more for electricity than necessary because they are using a distribution tariff that does not match their actual consumption.

A new analysis estimates that switching to a more suitable tariff could save households more than CZK 1.3 billion a year in total.

The analysis was conducted by energy company bezDodavatele.

The company examined electricity consumption at 1,132 household consumption points using the two most common household distribution tariffs, D01d and D02d.

According to data from the Energy Regulatory Office (ERÚ), D01d and D02d are used by around 65 percent of the approximately 6.5 million household consumption points in the Czech Republic.



The analysis found that changing the distribution tariff could reduce electricity costs for more than half of the households examined.

Many households never reconsider their tariff

One reason is that households often keep the same tariff for years without checking whether it still suits their electricity consumption.

A tariff that made sense when a household first connected to the electricity grid may no longer be the cheapest option after its consumption patterns have changed. Many consumers, however, do not regularly review the distribution tariff listed on their electricity bill.

According to the analysis, 53 percent of the households examined could have benefited from a different tariff. Their average potential saving was CZK 728 per year.

For some households, the difference was considerably larger, with potential savings reaching several thousand crowns annually.

Prague households show the highest potential

The analysis found differences between the country’s main electricity distribution areas.

In Prague, where electricity is distributed by PRE, changing the tariff could have been beneficial for 68 percent of the households included in the study. That was the highest proportion recorded among the three distribution zones.

In the EG.D distribution area, which covers much of southern Bohemia and Moravia as well as parts of the Vysočina, Zlín and Olomouc regions, the figure was 51.5 percent.

The lowest share was recorded in the ČEZ distribution area, where 46.3 percent of the households analyzed could potentially benefit from a different tariff.

The picture changes slightly when looking at the size of the potential savings. Although Prague had the highest proportion of households that could benefit from a tariff change, the largest average annual saving was recorded in the ČEZ Distribuce area, at CZK 833 per household.

World.title: Prague Welcomes STARLUX Airlines With New Taipei Connection
World.content:
Taiwanese carrier STARLUX Airlines has launched its first European route, connecting Taipei with Prague.

The airline’s first flight arrived at Václav Havel Airport Prague on Saturday morning after a journey of more than 14 hours. The service is initially being operated with an Airbus A350-900.

STARLUX plans to operate the Prague-Taipei route three times a week at first, with a fourth weekly service scheduled to be added from October.

For passengers traveling beyond Taiwan, the route also offers connections through Taipei to more than 25 destinations across Asia. These include cities in Japan and South Korea, as well as destinations in Southeast Asia, Hong Kong and Macau, according to Simon Liu, STARLUX Airlines’ director of strategy.

The new route makes Prague the airline’s first European destination. STARLUX launched operations only in 2020, two years after the company was founded, but has since positioned itself as a premium international carrier. Skytrax has awarded the airline a five-star rating.



A first-class cabin aimed at luxury travelers

STARLUX is introducing its Prague route with all four of its travel classes: Economy, Premium Economy, Business and First Class.

The First Class cabin has just four seats and comes with a price to match its exclusivity. Return fares can start at around $12,000, or roughly CZK 280,000, although prices vary depending on travel dates and other factors.

The experience begins before passengers reach the aircraft. First Class travelers departing from Prague can use an airport pickup service included with their ticket. In Taipei, the journey can continue with a limousine transfer from the airport to the passenger’s final destination.

Passengers also receive dedicated check-in facilities, priority airport processing and access to a private suite in the airline’s lounge.

On board, each First Class passenger has a private cabin with additional space and privacy, along with an enhanced dining and service offering.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by STARLUX Airlines (@starluxairlines)

Special AIRSORAYAMA aircraft coming to Prague

The aircraft serving Prague will also change later this year.

STARLUX plans to introduce its two specially designed AIRSORAYAMA Airbus A350-1000 aircraft on the Prague route. The planes were created in collaboration with Japanese artist Hajime Sorayama and feature metallic silver and gold liveries.

The airline has confirmed that the A350-1000 will replace the A350-900 on the Prague route from September. The two AIRSORAYAMA aircraft are scheduled to enter regular service on routes including Prague from October 1, when the airline also plans to introduce themed in-flight amenities.

The aircraft were created in partnership with Sorayama, whose work is known for its highly polished metallic representations of robots and the human form.

For Prague passengers, the arrival of the AIRSORAYAMA aircraft will add an unusual visual element to the new long-haul connection. The silver and gold A350-1000s are among STARLUX’s most distinctive aircraft and form part of the airline’s wider effort to combine aviation with contemporary design.

World.title: Lake Tisza under threat: alarm bells ring at tourist hotspot – photos
World.content:
The water level of Lake Tisza has fallen below 700 centimetres at the upper gauge at Kisköre. According to the Central Tisza Valley Water Directorate, the drop is due to an extreme lack of rainfall in the Tisza catchment area, exceptionally low river inflows and increased evaporation.

Lake Tisza exists because of irrigated arable farming

Water management specialists are working to preserve the available water resources while also meeting agricultural and ecological water demands, the water transfer in the Körös valley and the water supply for the stretch of the Tisza below Kisköre.

Lake Tisza is not a natural lake, but an artificial reservoir created in the Tisza floodplain. Its creation is linked to the Kisköre barrage, construction of which began in the late 1960s, while its hydroelectric equipment was completed by 1974. The dam primarily serves water storage, irrigation and water management tasks, while the resulting water surface has over time become home to an exceptionally rich ecosystem. The roughly 127-square-kilometre lake is fed by the Tisza, and its water level is influenced by the river’s flow and the operating regime of the water authorities.

Numerous tourism developments

In recent years, significant tourism developments have also taken place in the region. In Tiszafüred, the Lake Tisza Cycling Centre and the Tiszafüred–Poroszló cycle bridge were built, the open-water beach was renovated, and in 2024 new visitor attractions, including the Kérész Centre, also opened. Altogether 17 projects were carried out in the region in 2024, affecting tourist attractions, infrastructure and ecological conditions alike. A further 300 million forint development has also begun at Tiszafüred beach, including, among other things, a water playground, a cycling track and new services.

If you missed – The end draws near for Lake Velence as Danube hits a record low in Budapest: will Hungary dry out this year?

Today, Lake Tisza is a favourite destination for cyclists, water tourists, anglers and swimmers. The cycle route around the lake can be completed safely, while visitors can discover the reeds, islands and channels on boat and canoe trips. In addition to swimming, there are opportunities for nature watching and fishing. The current drop in water level is therefore an important issue not only for water management, but also for tourism.

Magyar government unveils 12-point plan to save Lake Velence after water levels hit historic lows

World.title: Will Fidesz split soon? A survey says the breakaway camp would have a strong chance
World.content:
Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party seemed only a few months ago to be a monolithic bloc, unassailable at the summit of power. Now, however, it appears it could even split in two: into an Orbán party and a moderate, centre-right grouping. A fresh Medián poll may now give that scenario another push.

A new civic party would stand a good chance

Medián Research Institute is the only Hungarian polling company to have accurately predicted the results of every parliamentary and European Parliament election, and it also pinpointed the scale of Tisza’s April victory with remarkable precision, assigning Péter Magyar’s movement exactly the number of seats it ultimately won.

On the basis of the latest Medián survey, if former Fidesz politicians who represented a moderate, civic line were to found a new party, they would make it into parliament. Of course, that is meagre consolation in light of the party’s former multi-million vote hauls and two-thirds majorities: sitting in opposition in the Hungarian National Assembly under current conditions is useful at best for paying politicians and their assistants, while against governing parties armed with a two-thirds majority the chances of any real success are slim.

Having 5-10 MPs against 141 is not easy, but being in the Parliament has its advantages. Photo: Facebook/TISZA Párt

In any case, Medián says a new civic force would be able to appeal to at least 5 per cent of the total population. Had such a party existed in April, then according to the poll summarised by hvg.hu it would have been the third-largest group in parliament, ahead of Mi Hazánk.

Many Fidesz voters are only loosely tied to Orbán

Names have also been mentioned in connection with the new formation. Among public figures seen as part of Fidesz’s moderate wing — and critical of the party leadership according to both the news and their own remarks — atv.hu cited former EC commissioner and minister Tibor Navracsics, Székesfehérvár mayor András Cser-Palkovics, and former MP and government commissioner Orsolya Ferenc.

Will Orbán’s Fidesz split? Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

Interestingly, according to Median, only one third of current Fidesz supporters remain firmly loyal to Viktor Orban, while 18 per cent would have no problem switching to the new party, and 15 per cent would at least consider it. The new party could therefore potentially count on roughly one third of Fidesz’s existing camp — which stands at around 19-20 per cent support — but that would indeed be enough to clear the parliamentary threshold, at least under the current rules.

Former Orbán spin doctor, Árpád Habony, appears to have left Hungary, new address reveals

A rock-solid Tisza lead

Tisza, meanwhile, has promised a new electoral law, which is also a social expectation of them. Within that framework they are already talking about a number of innovations, including limits on MPs as well. The more hardline camp would allow anyone to sit in parliament for just two terms, while the more permissive would allow three terms, or 12 years. All this also means that Mi Hazánk’s caucus could be completely replaced, while within Fidesz’s parliamentary group replacements are already under way so that those who still see a future in parliamentary work can take on the government across the chamber.

Tisza continues to enjoy support unseen before among Hungarian voters: 57 per cent of the total population would back it in an election held this Sunday.

Péter Magyar’s lead is rock-solid. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

World.title: Ancient suburban rail carriages to be replaced soon, Hungarian minister vows
World.content:
As part of the Baross Gábor Rail Development Plan, the 50-year-old suburban rail carriages will be replaced, with the procurement process for the renewal of the entire HÉV fleet on the H5 Szentendre, H6 Ráckeve and H7 Csepel lines due to be launched this year, Dávid Vitézy, the transport and investment minister, wrote in a Facebook post on Wednesday.

42 new suburban rail carriages

He said 42 new, modern, 120-metre-long trainsets will be purchased using EU funds returned to Hungary. The necessary tender will be issued later this year, and the first trains could enter service in 2030.

The fleet will be upgraded with fully accessible, air-conditioned, modern vehicles, offering passengers a more comfortable, faster and more reliable service, he added.

Currently, Budapest and its surrounding areas are served by four HÉV lines: H5 (Szentendre), H6 (Ráckeve), H7 (Csepel), and H8–H9 (Gödöllő and Csömör). Photo: Kemény Máté / Wikimedia Commons

He said that in recent years hundreds of thousands of people have moved from the countryside to Budapest, and from the capital to the surrounding commuter belt and outer districts, often without adequate public transport links. As a result, traffic has continued to grow, and Budapest’s inner city has become increasingly difficult in which to live.

The only real remedy, he wrote, is high-quality public transport, and one of the key conditions is that HÉV should offer a genuine alternative to the car in terms of comfort, quality and speed.

World.title: Putin’s people take aim at PM Magyar again, this time mocking the energy crisis and Paks
World.content:
The country has spent days anxiously awaiting news of whether the entire Paks nuclear power plant will have to be shut down, or whether Unit 2, which produces 240MW, can continue operating at reduced output. While the signs are now encouraging, the Russians nevertheless appear to have decided this was the moment to take a swipe at Péter Magyar, who had previously criticised the Russian-run Paks II development as too expensive.

Russians write about difficulties at Paks and Romania’s Cernavoda

“Mr Magyar, do you still think it is too expensive?” the Russian state news agency RIA Novosti reportedly told the prime minister yesterday, according to atv.hu. Operations at the Paks nuclear plant have been hanging by a thread, but it now appears the Danube will not continue to fall, meaning Unit 2 may remain operational at half power for several more days — just when electricity is needed most to keep the country functioning.

In a longer report, the Russian state agency analyses the situation at Hungarian and Romanian nuclear plants, highlighting that both use water from the Danube for cooling. As a result, not only the amount of water available matters, but also the river’s temperature, since discharged water at high temperatures cannot be returned to the river in the interests of protecting wildlife.

Both the Paks and Cernavoda plants are operating at sharply reduced capacity, with a single unit carrying the load at both sites at lower output. The Romanians carried out a major detonation in the Danube the day before yesterday to help supply their plant, as we reported separately with video. In Paks, there is cause for optimism because the drop in the Danube’s water level appears to have stopped. In Budapest, for example, it has risen by 11cm from its low point. At one stage, the shutdown of Paks yesterday morning came down to mere millimetres.

The Danube at the Paks NPP. Photo: MTI

Russian agency takes a swipe at Péter Magyar

Against this backdrop, the Russian state news agency evidently felt it important to take a dig at the Hungarian prime minister, criticising between the lines his sceptical stance on the Paks II development. Péter Magyar had previously indicated that the project’s costs and contractual framework would be subject to a comprehensive review before any final decision is taken.

Paks II NPP extension project. Photo: Facebook/Csárdi Antal

The Russians now pointed to how important Paks is in Hungary’s energy mix — around 40 per cent — and how significant the new blocks would be in future, though it should be noted that they too would rely on Danube water, and would also have to be shut down in the event of drought. Rosatom had previously said it was ready to take part in an audit of the Paks II project so that the Hungarian side could make an informed decision as soon as possible.

If you missed – Horror over Paks II NPP overpricing: did Orbán-linked and Tisza-affiliated businessmen and politicians pocket the cash?

Shifting Hungarian-Russian ties

Hungarian-Russian relations have become rather chilly since Tisza’s election victory. The Russians signalled that they were ready to continue pragmatic ties, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov even singled out Magyar for praise for the fact that Hungary still does not send weapons to Ukraine. The mocking tone of the latest news agency report may therefore come as something of a surprise.

Former PM Putin in Moscow with President Putin. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

During the campaign, Péter Magyar repeatedly spoke of Russian interference on the side of Fidesz — with evidence, for example, cited by journalist Szabolcs Panyi — as President Putin had previously backed Orbán. Since his election victory, however, Magyar has struck a pragmatically detached tone, emphasising his commitment to NATO and the EU, and has called on Putin to end the killing in Ukraine.
