Fear of punishment may encourage people to censor themselves. This effect is particularly visible on platforms such as TikTok, where younger users may begin avoiding sensitive topics and refrain from expressing critical or unconventional views. As a result, the space for public debate narrows and the diversity of opinions declines. The principles of necessity and proportionality: Even if protecting public morality is accepted as a legitimate aim, any restrictions must be necessary and proportionate to that objective. Administrative detention ranging from eight to 30 days may appear relatively short. However, its systematic and frequent use can turn punishment into a tool of control. Given the availability of alternative measures, such as warnings, platform moderation policies and media literacy programmes, the necessity of depriving people of their liberty raises important legal questions.

TikTok arrests in Azerbaijan

World.title: From “rapid response” to possible law: who are Georgia’s national values being protected from?
World.content:
The Georgian government has not ruled out introducing legislation against what it describes as the erosion of national identity. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the proposed rules could cover insults directed at saints, monarchs and prominent public figures. No draft law has been introduced yet. However, experts argue that the groundwork is already being laid. Members of the ruling team have already begun discussing penalties and possible regulation of the media.

As the ruling Georgian Dream party debates possible punishment for insulting national values, it is worth examining what such measures could cover and what Russia’s experience suggests.

From assaults to a campaign to “protect national values”

The debate over possible legislation followed an attack on comedian Onise Okriashvili over a joke he made on YouTube. Late on 22 July, a man assaulted him near his home in Tbilisi. The attacker, Niko Khurtsilava, said he acted because Okriashvili had insulted Georgian national culture.

Even before the assault, pro-government television channels had launched a media campaign against Okriashvili. They broadcast a clipped excerpt from his YouTube show in which he referred to renowned Georgian writer Nodar Dumbadze using obscene language.

The writer’s grandson, Nodar Macharashvili, publicly backed the attacker. A few days after the incident, MMA fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, who also described himself as Khurtsilava’s friend, announced the creation of a new movement that would provide “rapid response” to insults directed at sacred values, ancestors, religion and history.

“If protecting our culture and national identity requires it, we will not shy away from any threat. We are ready to take responsibility for every action we take and, if necessary, even go to prison,” Kartvelishvili said.

He did not specify what he meant by “rapid response”. He also declined to answer journalists’ questions about the use of physical violence and vigilantism.

On 28 July, the group applied to the Public Registry to register its newly established organisation under the name National Generation.

A week after the attack on Okriashvili, on 30 July, another initiative group emerged to “protect national values”. It brought together actor Giorgi Shanidze, director Giorgi Sikharulidze and Kote Mzhavia, director of the Batumi Theatre.

Unlike the first movement, this group called for legal mechanisms rather than “rapid response”. Its members said the law should protect the church, sacred sites, historical heroes and national values.

“Freedom of expression is a fundamental value. However, that right cannot become a tool for insulting the sacred symbols and core values that form the country’s historical, cultural and spiritual foundation,” Giorgi Shanidze said.

The statement refers to “externally funded destructive groups” whose activities, it says, are creating confrontation between the Georgian nation and small minority groups.

“To prevent the situation from escalating further and reaching the point where even the wise Georgian people could lose patience, responsible steps must be taken and the existing problems must be resolved through legal and peaceful means,” the statement says.

The group plans to hold consultations with lawyers, historians, artists and athletes before drafting a legislative proposal.

However, neither the bill nor its concept has been published, so it remains unclear which actions could become punishable. The proposed form of liability and possible penalties also remain unknown.

What could a law on national values include?

On 3 August, Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that he did not rule out adopting such legislation. However, he said the authorities had not yet discussed any specific proposals.

“There is indeed a need to respond to the coordinated attack against our identity,” Kobakhidze said.

He also identified possible subjects of future regulation, including saints, kings and prominent public figures.

According to Kobakhidze, insults directed at Georgian saints and kings are part of “a chain of coordinated, commissioned actions.”

“These are not simply untalented people. These are people carrying out a specific assignment. The purpose of that assignment is simple: they are trying to weaken our national identity. That is why they are doing all this,” he said.

Kobakhidze did not specify who had allegedly commissioned the campaign. He also provided no evidence to support the claim.

“We must take every possible measure to counter such processes. If that requires adopting a law, we can discuss that as well.”

Kobakhidze’s remarks do not necessarily mean such a law will be adopted. However, they indicate that the initiative has already received political backing from the prime minister.

Meanwhile, MPs aligned with the ruling party have outlined possible restrictions in greater detail.

Georgian Dream MP Irakli Kadagishvili linked the issue to public swearing, abusive language and hooliganism.

“When people use obscene language against a specific individual or institution at a rally, is that freedom of expression or simply abusive language and hooliganism? We cannot just leave it like this.”

Kadagishvili said he did not know what the legislation might ultimately contain. At the same time, he suggested that the media could also fall within its scope.

The MP claimed that certain television channels — referring to opposition broadcasters — had aired 3,500 “anti-church” reports over the past year and a half. He did not explain how he arrived at that figure or what criteria he used to classify the reports as “anti-church”.

Kadagishvili also suggested that “offensive” media content could become subject to legal regulation.

Guram Macharashvili, a member of the People’s Power party, openly called for penalties for public insults. He said the law should protect faith, the church, the patriarch and national traditions.

“When you publicly insult values such as faith, the church, the patriarch or our traditions, that should, of course, be punishable.”

Macharashvili argued that Georgia had offered excessive protection to dissenting views.

“Dissent has always enjoyed a certain degree of protection in Georgia. But recently, I would say it has been protected in an ultra-liberal, excessive way, and that needs to change.”

What counts as an “insult” — and who decides?

Article 17 of Georgia’s Constitution guarantees freedom of thought and expression. It also prohibits persecution for expressing an opinion.

The constitution also guarantees media freedom and prohibits censorship.

The state may restrict freedom of expression only by law and only when necessary in a democratic society. Such restrictions may serve aims including public safety and the protection of other people’s rights. The constitution does not list “insulting national values” as a separate ground for limiting freedom of expression.

At the same time, freedom of expression is not absolute. The law may restrict incitement to violence, threats, harassment or defamation. However, such restrictions must be clearly defined and predictable.

By contrast, “insulting national values” is a far more ambiguous concept. It remains unclear whether the proposed law would protect the reputation of specific individuals or instead safeguard abstract values or historical figures.

It is also unclear who would decide which saints, kings and public figures deserve legal protection. Would the law apply only to historical figures? Where would the line be drawn between legitimate historical criticism and an “insult”?

For example, pro-government television channels also launched a campaign against literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili after he criticised the policies of Georgian King Erekle II. Berdzenishvili neither joked about the king nor used obscene language. Nevertheless, Georgian Dream MPs and pro-government media sharply attacked him.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed restrictions would apply to satire, works of art or academic research. Another unanswered question is whether critical media coverage of members of the clergy could be treated as an “insult to sacred values”.

Protecting patriotism or deepening political divisions?

Opposition politicians see the initiative as an attempt to mobilise political support.

Giorgi Sharashidze of the For Georgia party argues that the government is trying to claim a monopoly on patriotism.

“They have a very calculated strategy — to gain exclusive ownership of patriotic issues. Everything serves that goal. They want everyone else to appear as opponents of Georgia’s identity, traditions and church, while presenting themselves as the sole defenders of those values.”

Giorgi Shalamberidze of the First Georgia party believes the proposed law could serve another political purpose.

“It could be a political manoeuvre. It may help mobilise a particular segment of voters, or it could mark the beginning of a much broader tightening of legislation in the long term.”

Shalamberidze acknowledged that freedom of expression can be restricted in certain circumstances. However, he pointed to Georgia’s current political environment.

“If this becomes law and is used as a tool, the question is how it will affect political actors, political parties and their freedom of expression, and to what extent it will become a mechanism for restricting their rights.”

Historians’ concerns

It remains unclear where the proposed law would draw the line between insulting a historical figure and offering a critical assessment. That uncertainty raises concerns for historians, researchers and authors.

Assessing historical figures often requires revisiting disputed facts, competing interpretations and long-established narratives.

If the state decides which interpretations are acceptable, the law could become a tool for restricting academic research and scholarly debate.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed rules would apply to academic publications, public lectures, textbooks or documentary films.

Another unanswered question is who would decide where legitimate historical criticism ends and an “insult” begins.

Historian Irakli Khvadagiani argues that placing faith and artistic expression into legal categories contradicts their very nature.

“Faith and creativity do not recognise prohibitions, nor do they accept categories imposed unilaterally. The idea of banning them through legislation is absurd. Humanity went through this centuries ago. It is simply the obsession of a dictator trying to bend society to his will.”

Risk of creating artificial divisions?

Conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili believes the proposed legislation could fuel ethnic and religious tensions. In his view, the vague concept of “protecting national identity” risks creating new fault lines within society.

“There are not enough supporters of this ideology in Georgia for Georgian Dream to sustain permanent tensions between Christians and Muslims, between Georgians and non-Georgians, or between Georgian speakers and those who do not speak the language.”

Zakareishvili sees elements of far-right ideology in the government’s approach. He argues that it runs counter to the principles of equality and justice.

“This is a classic example of pure far-right ideology. Humanity has gone through this countless times, and it has repeatedly led to catastrophe and world wars, bringing nothing but destruction.”

The conflict analyst also links the initiative to the electoral cycle. Georgia’s next parliamentary elections are not due until October 2028. However, Zakareishvili believes the ruling party has already begun preparing its campaign.

“Georgian Dream is getting ready for the elections. Before the vote, it needs to create exactly these kinds of flashpoints.”

Cases of violence carried out in the name of “protecting traditions” Invoking the need to protect national and religious values is not a new phenomenon in Georgian politics. In 2023, a man attacked Zurab Japaridze, leader of the Girchi – More Freedom party, in the city of Gori. The attacker said he acted because Japaridze had insulted the church and was “corrupting children”.

Later that year, protesters disrupted a lecture by Levan Berdzenishvili in Kvareli. They accused him of insulting King Erekle II and Christian values. In Tbilisi, demonstrators also threw eggs at Berdzenishvili.

On 5 July 2021, opponents of Tbilisi Pride attacked journalists and activists. They justified the violence by saying they were defending the family, the church and traditional values. More than 50 journalists were injured.

In November 2019, far-right and anti-LGBT groups tried to disrupt the premiere of the film And Then We Danced. The Georgian Orthodox Church described the film as “an insult to Georgia’s traditional values”. Protesters attempted to storm cinemas. One of them threw a stone at civil activist Anna Subeliani, causing a serious head injury. Police arrested 12 people that evening.

In January 2024, activist Nata Peradze splashed paint on an icon in Tbilisi’s Holy Trinity Cathedral depicting Saint Matrona of Moscow alongside Joseph Stalin. Far-right groups later gathered outside Peradze’s home, demanding that she be punished.

On 17 May 2013, thousands of people, including members of the clergy, attacked participants in an anti-homophobia rally. At least 17 people were injured. In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the violence had taken place in circumstances of the state’s effective acquiescence.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is particularly relevant in this context because the substance and rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia years earlier.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially justified their version as a tool to ensure transparency over foreign funding. They later expanded it into a mechanism used against independent media outlets and civil society organisations.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is relevant here because both the substance and the rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia in recent years.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially presented their version as a transparency measure for foreign funding. They later expanded it into a tool used against independent media and civil society organisations.

It is therefore worth looking at how Russia gradually developed legislation under the banner of protecting “traditional values”, religious feelings and historical memory.

Russia did not build its legal framework for protecting religion, historical memory and “traditional values” overnight. The system evolved step by step.

Offending religious feelings

In 2012, members of the punk group Pussy Riot staged an anti-Vladimir Putin performance inside Moscow’s Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. A court convicted them of hooliganism motivated by religious hatred.

A year later, Russia toughened Article 148 of its Criminal Code by criminalising public acts that show clear disrespect for society and are committed with the intention of offending the religious feelings of believers.

One of the best-known cases under the law involved blogger Ruslan Sokolovsky, who filmed himself playing Pokémon Go inside a church and posted the video online. In other videos, he also criticised religion and the Russian Orthodox Church.

In 2017, a court gave Sokolovsky a three-and-a-half-year suspended prison sentence. The case involved several criminal charges, including offending believers’ religious feelings and inciting hatred.

In 2024, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Sokolovsky’s conviction had violated his right to freedom of expression. The court found that offensive or vulgar speech does not automatically amount to hate speech.

“Traditional values” as state policy

In November 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on protecting “traditional Russian spiritual and moral values”.

The document lists patriotism, dignity, life and the traditional family among those values. It also includes service to the fatherland, historical memory and continuity between generations.

According to the decree, external forces threaten these values by acting inside Russia through extremist and terrorist organisations.

The decree also identifies the United States and other “unfriendly states” as sources of those threats.

Russian authorities have explicitly linked cultural and values policy to national security.

A similar narrative has emerged in Georgian Dream’s campaign. Both initiative groups have spoken of a coordinated attack on Georgia’s “national identity”. Prime Minister Kobakhidze has used the same wording.

Legal protection of history

Article 354.1 of Russia’s Criminal Code is titled “Rehabilitation of Nazism”. Lawmakers originally introduced it to prohibit the denial of crimes established by the Nuremberg Tribunal.

However, the law goes much further. It also bans the dissemination of what authorities consider to be “knowingly false information” about the Soviet Union’s actions during the Second World War. The article also protects the honour and dignity of war veterans.

In 2021, lawmakers added a new offence covering the “insulting of the memory of the defenders of the Fatherland”. The law also criminalises offensive use of military glory symbols.

As a result, the legislation does more than prohibit denial of historical facts. It also protects the state’s official interpretation of the Soviet Union’s role in history.

According to a 2025 study by the human rights project OVD-Info, Russian courts handed down 25 convictions under Article 354.1 between 2015 and 2019. Many of the cases concerned interpretations of the Soviet Union’s actions and historical comparisons.

Between 2022 and May 2025, OVD-Info recorded 212 prosecutions under the same article.

A court gave Kazan resident Zulfiya Sitdikova a two-year suspended sentence over posters reading “No to war” and “9 Way”. She replaced the “M” in “May” with a “W”, and investigators interpreted this as desecration of Victory Day symbols.

Authorities also opened a criminal case against historian Mikhail Belousov. Investigators accused him of denying facts established by the Nuremberg Tribunal and spreading false information about the Soviet Union.

Prosecutors also opened two cases against historian Tamara Eidelman. They argued that her video lectures showed disrespect for Russia’s military remembrance days.

Russia has therefore created a system in which historians and society no longer have the final say in historical debates. Instead, investigators, expert witnesses and the courts have become the ultimate arbiters.

Where will Georgia draw the line?

Georgia has not yet introduced such a bill, so it is impossible to say whether it will follow the Russian path.

However, statements by members of the ruling party already suggest a broad range of protected subjects, including the church, the patriarch, saints, kings, public figures, traditions and even media content.

Russia’s experience also suggests that broadly defined protected values can gradually expand over time.

Protecting national values in Georgia

World.title: Georgian scam call centres: old fraudsters, new address? An investigation
World.content:
Georgian scam call centres that came under the spotlight during an international investigative project in 2025 have reportedly resumed operations from a new location. According to the investigative outlet Monitor, people linked to AK Group have relocated to an office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street in Tbilisi.

The outlet says its journalists conducted covert surveillance at the address for six months. They say they identified several of the same individuals who had been seen near AK Group’s previous office last year. According to Monitor, the footage also shows some of the same vehicles that regularly appeared at the company’s former location.

Journalists say they repeatedly spotted vehicles used by Akaki Kevkhishvili, who is widely believed to be the real operator of AK Group. The cars carried the registration numbers AK100KK and AK200KK. Investigators seized one of them in 2025 as part of the ongoing criminal investigation.

According to Monitor, AK Group’s registered owner and director, Meri Shotadze, also regularly visited the same address. She used two different vehicles, one of which investigators have also seized, while the other is registered to another person.

The investigation also claims that several agents who previously worked at AK Group’s former office have reappeared at the new location. They include Anzhelika Chkhapelia, who allegedly used the alias Marina Novikova; Misha Bayramov; Valerian Gigauri; Giorgi Gotman; and Ketevan Malashkhia, who allegedly used the alias Ashley Moriarty. According to Monitor, Malashkhia is a cousin of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife. The outlet also identified a Belarusian citizen, Lita, who had previously denied working at the call centre.

The journalists also say they identified security staff at the new office who had previously been seen outside AK Group’s former premises. They named former law enforcement officer Manuchar Gegia and former Zugdidi traffic police chief Levan Gogia.

According to the outlet, the office on Mirian Mepe Street closed after it announced the publication of its latest investigation. Both floors of the building are now being offered for rent.

Monitor says the premises had been leased since 2022 by RTM Imports, a company owned by Irakli Kvlividze, the brother of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife.

The journalists say they informed the Prosecutor’s Office on 1 July 2026 that AK Group’s managers and employees had been regularly operating from the office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street. According to Monitor, prosecutors have not clarified whether they investigated the information or whether the inquiry into the alleged fraud is still ongoing.

Background

In 2025, Monitor and more than 32 international media organisations published an investigation into AK Group’s activities. According to the report, the group employed 85 people and defrauded more than 6,100 people across Europe and Canada between 2022 and 2025. The journalists estimated that the operation generated more than $35 million in revenue over that period.

After the investigation was published, law enforcement authorities opened a criminal inquiry into organised fraud and the laundering of proceeds from crime on an especially large scale. Prosecutors have charged 11 people in the case.

In a separate bribery case, authorities also arrested former Georgian State Security Service chief Grigol Liluashvili. Prosecutors accuse him, in one of the counts, of providing protection to the call centres. A court has also frozen the assets and company shares of the alleged organisers and employees of the call centre network.

Investigation continues

According to Monitor, the Prosecutor’s Office told the outlet that it had requested legal assistance from Germany to help identify potential victims. Prosecutors also said they had sought additional information from journalists involved in the investigation, but claimed they had declined to cooperate.

In a written response, the Prosecutor’s Office said that “the final decision in the case largely depends on information and materials to be obtained from abroad through legal assistance.”

A separate Monitor investigation found that Akaki Kevkhishvili and Meri Shotadze had previously worked at another call centre, 100 Marketing Solutions. Authorities began investigating the company in 2023 and froze its shares as part of the inquiry. However, a court lifted the freeze in 2026.

Are Georgian scam call centres still operating?

World.title: Armenia approves new government as Pashinyan promises appointments based on merit
World.content:
Armenia approves new government

Alongside the opening of Armenia‘s 9th parliamentary term, the country formed a new government. In line with the constitution, Nikol Pashinyan took office as prime minister. He headed the electoral list of the Civil Contract party, which won a parliamentary majority.

The party submitted the required nomination documents for its leader to President Vahagn Khachaturyan, who then signed a decree appointing Pashinyan as prime minister.

On the previous day, at the proposal of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and by decree of President Vahagn Khachaturyan, Deputy Prime Ministers Mher Grigoryan and Tigran Khachatryan were reappointed to their posts.

Most cabinet ministers were also reappointed.

Changes were made in the prime minister’s office. Former chief adviser to the prime minister and former Armenian ambassador to the United States, Lilit Makunts, has been appointed chief of staff. Her predecessor, Araik Harutyunyan, became an MP with the ruling Civil Contract faction on August 2.

At the same time, Pashinyan announced that he plans to appoint graduates of leading universities from around the world, selected through the government’s talent pool, to senior positions in the government.

“You will soon see these decisions implemented in practice,” the prime minister said.

Almost all ministers kept their portfolios

At Prime Minister Pashinyan’s recommendation, the following ministers retained their posts:

Defence – Suren Papikyan,

Internal Affairs – Arpine Sargsyan,

Foreign Affairs – Ararat Mirzoyan,

Territorial Administration and Infrastructure – David Khudatyan,

Environment – Hambardzum Matevosyan,

Health – Anahit Avanesyan,

Education, Science, Culture and Sport – Zhanna Andreasyan,

Justice – Srbuhi Galyan,

Labour and Social Affairs – Arsen Torosyan,

Economy – Gevorg Papoyan,

Finance – Vahe Hovhannisyan.

Only High-Tech Industry Minister Mkhitar Hayrapetyan did not keep his post. Pashinyan had previously said that Hayrapetyan himself had decided to step down.

David Tadevosyan replaced him. The prime minister introduced the new minister to ministry staff today. Mkhitar Hayrapetyan also attended the meeting. He said he would remain available around the clock if the new minister or his team needed advice.

“I am ready to contribute my modest knowledge and experience whenever you feel the need,” the former minister said.

David Tadevosyan graduated from the National Polytechnic University of Armenia. Between 2012 and 2014, he studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he earned a Master of Science in Engineering and Management.

Before taking up the ministerial post, Tadevosyan served as acting director of International Radio Network CJSC. Between 2024 and 2025, he headed Afeyan Initiatives for Armenia, an organisation founded by Armenian-American businessman, scientist and philanthropist Noubar Afeyan. Earlier in his career, Tadevosyan worked for the mining company Vallex Group, the Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Chemical Technologies, and SberSpinoff.

More than 1,000 applications for the government’s talent pool

On 15 June, shortly after his Civil Contract party won the 2026 parliamentary elections, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan invited graduates of the world’s leading universities to join the government. He encouraged them to put their knowledge and professional experience to work in public administration.

Today, the prime minister said the initiative had attracted strong interest, with the government receiving 1,141 applications.

“Following the initial screening, 459 candidates – around 40% of all applicants – advanced to the second stage. The average age of the candidates is 34,” Pashinyan said.

The prime minister announced that the government would create a talent pool based on interview results and professional assessments. Officials will match the selected candidates’ education, work experience and professional skills with the specific needs of the public administration system.

He added that candidates included in the talent pool could receive offers for positions in the public sector or other forms of cooperation during the course of this year.

Armenia approves new government

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘It’s important to understand what kind of hell government is leading us into’
World.content:
Lasha Tugushi, head of the Liberal Academy, has commented on Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s claim that Georgian politicians have never used harsher rhetoric towards Russia than they do today, either before or after the 2008 war. Tugushi argues that the prime minister is repeating a familiar narrative promoted by the ruling Georgian Dream party.

According to Tugushi, the government is trying to present itself as the only force capable of “saving” the country, while linking the events of 2008 and 2022 forms part of that political strategy.

According to Tugushi, the suggestion that Georgia was ever pro-Russian is “nonsense”, as portraying Russia in a positive light has always been regarded as shameful in Georgian society.

Earlier, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy social media statement linking the war in Ukraine to Georgia’s domestic politics and the country’s opposition. According to Kobakhidze, the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine in order to “fuel Russophobia among its agents around the world, including in Georgia, at the highest level.”

Lasha Tugushi said: “Anti-Russian sentiment existed in Georgia long before this. I remember the 1990s, when hostility towards Russia was very strong. The same was true after the war in Abkhazia. I cannot agree with the prime minister’s view that the key turning points were 2008 and 2022.

“I do not remember Georgia ever being pro-Russian. That is nonsense. What’s more, in respectable society it has always been considered shameful to say that Russia is a good country or to speak positively about Russian symbols.

“As for the focus on 2008 and 2022, that is part of a political game in which the leaders of Georgian Dream repeat a familiar narrative: that there is only one benevolent political force capable of saving Georgia – Georgian Dream. Everyone else, they claim, is either an enemy or a traitor seeking to drag the country into a devastating war.”

“But let’s remember who suspended Georgia’s EU integration, who is pursuing an anti-European policy today, who is confronting the ambassadors of Western countries, the European Parliament and the OSCE, who is picking fights with Sweden and France. Who came up with the scare story about the ‘deep state’? Georgian Dream did all of that.

“That does not mean the previous government made no mistakes or that everything was perfect. We need to understand that politics cannot be viewed in black-and-white terms. Things should be called by their proper names. The previous government has plenty of its own sins, and it paid the price for them. But today we see countries that were once on a par with Georgia moving closer to EU membership, while we, instead of advancing towards integration, are drifting further away from the West.”

“There are two main pillars on which the current government relies.

The first is fear – the claim that enemies want to open a second front in Georgia.

The second is the argument that our Georgian identity is under threat.

These are the two narratives they use to frighten people and rely on a fearful public in order to remain in power indefinitely.

But the fact is that they are not succeeding in their campaign against democracy to the extent they would like. It is crucial to see clearly what kind of hell this government is leading us into and what it actually looks like.

Over the past few years, Georgian Dream has taken many steps backwards and not a single step forward. This is an anti-national path. It is building authoritarianism and working against the Georgian people. I have many questions. For example, can Georgian Dream correct the grave mistakes it has made? I would like to believe it can find that path and that at least something will change.”

On Georgian Dream’s policies

World.title: Georgian PM: ‘Opposition’s current Russophobia is dictated by Global War Party’
World.content:
Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has published a lengthy social media statement linking Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine to Georgia‘s domestic politics and the country’s opposition.

According to Kobakhidze, the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine in order to “fuel Russophobia among its agents around the world, including in Georgia, at the highest level.”

Kobakhidze writes that after the war in Ukraine began in 2022, the “opposition’s pseudo-liberal minority” in Georgia adopted a radical stance towards Russia. He argues that such attitudes had not existed even after the August 2008 war, despite the fact that Russia continued to occupy 20% of Georgia’s territory.

In his statement, the prime minister recalls the consequences of the 2008 war. He says Russia’s military aggression killed 412 people, injured 2,232 others and displaced about 30,000 people. More than 120 Georgian settlements also remained beyond the occupation line.

Kobakhidze argues that the United National Movement, which was in power at the time, did not pursue a hard-line policy towards Russia. Instead, he says, it encouraged Russian tourists and investors to come to Georgia, promoted cultural and economic ties, facilitated Russian investment in various sectors and later unilaterally abolished visa requirements for Russian citizens.

According to the prime minister, neither government officials nor their supporters protested against that policy at the time. In this context, Kobakhidze names several current opposition politicians and public figures, including Elene Khoshtaria and Zurab Japaridze, and claims they supported closer relations with Russia during that period.

According to the prime minister, the opposition, along with affiliated NGOs and activists, turned into an “externally controlled network of agents” and adopted a sharply anti-Russian stance only after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Kobakhidze argues that the Georgian opposition’s current “Russophobia” is not genuine but stems from “directives issued by external forces”. He says that if anyone were to develop a truly radical attitude towards Russia, it should have happened after the August 2008 war, not after Russia’s second invasion of Ukraine.

The prime minister concludes his statement by asking why this “network of agents” did not display the same attitude towards Russia after the 2008 war, but only after the war in Ukraine began. Kobakhidze says society “will easily find a logical explanation” for that question.

“I believe there is a question that must be asked and carefully considered by society. We all know that, both in the past and today, this network of agents in Georgia has acted on instructions from external forces, and that its homeland is not Georgia but the ‘deep state’.

Against that backdrop, it is worth asking why they were not instructed to promote Russophobia when there was the strongest possible reason to do so – after the August 2008 war – and why they have been instructed to do so now, when the victim of Russian aggression is not their formal homeland but another country, albeit a friendly one. I believe society will easily find a logical explanation for this contradiction,” Kobakhidze wrote.

Kobakhidze on Russophobia in Georgia

World.title: Diaspora youth: Patriots or ‘information soldiers’? The hidden mission of camp in Azerbaijan
World.content:
Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan

Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan. More than 120 young people from 64 countries gathered in Zangilan under the slogan “Reviving Cities”. Officials told participants they should defend Azerbaijan’s achievements and push back against what they described as “biased campaigns”.

Against the backdrop of protesters calling Ilham Aliyev a “dictator” in Berlin, that message raises another question: is the state seeking to foster independent thinkers or “information soldiers” who will promote its official narrative abroad?

What was discussed at the 7th Diaspora Youth Summer Camp?

The 7th Diaspora Youth Summer Camp, which opened in Zangilan on 2 August, is officially presented as a platform for “patriotic education”, learning about “the realities on the ground” and rejuvenating the Azerbaijani diaspora. More than 120 young people from 64 countries are spending a week visiting reconstruction projects in the territories retaken by Azerbaijan, meeting government officials and learning what organisers describe as “Azerbaijani realities”.

A closer look at the speeches by Fuad Muradov, chairman of the State Committee for Work with the Diaspora, and other officials, however, reveals a more pragmatic objective. The government appears to see young people living abroad not simply as members of the diaspora with ties to their homeland, but as active participants in the information battle.

Muradov said the participants should be able to “respond with well-founded arguments to biased campaigns”. He said they should “represent” Azerbaijan’s interests with dignity in their countries of residence, on international platforms and within their own communities.

Another message struck an even tougher tone. Officials said that although their number was small, some people living abroad who called themselves Azerbaijanis did not welcome Azerbaijan’s successes. They urged participants to know who these people were, be familiar with their statements and respond to them with well-reasoned arguments. Officials also said “black PR”, “distortion of facts” and “organised campaigns” were unacceptable. At the same time, they said they remained open to “well-founded criticism”.

Elvin Aslanov, a representative of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, acknowledged that defending Azerbaijan abroad was “far from easy”, saying it required confronting double standards and disinformation. According to him, the young participants’ mission is to “convey the truth accurately and objectively”.

From the authorities’ perspective, such rhetoric may appear defensive and entirely legitimate. However, the broader context allows for another interpretation. Critics argue that the programme goes beyond patriotic education and instead systematically prepares “information soldiers” – young people expected to promote the official narrative on social media, in online discussions and in international debates. In other words, they see it as an attempt to build a state-directed “soft power” network.

What happened in Berlin, and why does it matter in this context?

The timing of these appeals is no coincidence. During Ilham Aliyev’s official visit to Germany on 21 July, Azerbaijani expatriates gathered on the streets of Berlin and chanted: “Dictator!”

Around the same time, Germany-based exiled blogger Alemdar Bunyatov approached Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and presidential aide Hikmet Hajiyev on a street in Berlin. He questioned them about political prisoners and allegations of torture.

Official media immediately described the incident as a “provocation” and portrayed Bunyatov as someone “known for his close ties to the Iranian intelligence services”. Responding to his questions, Bayramov dismissed the allegations of torture as “a personal opinion”.

Hajiyev, for his part, questioned Bunyatov about his sources of funding, his legal status in Germany and his reasons for leaving Azerbaijan. He stressed the importance of sovereignty and national security. The incident triggered a strong reaction in pro-government media, which portrayed the blogger’s questions as “provocative”.

The events in Berlin further illustrate the practical meaning of the messages delivered in Zangilan. In the official narrative, criticism is often framed as a “biased campaign”, “black PR” or the result of “external influence”.

As a result, the authorities themselves largely determine the line between “well-founded criticism” and a “biased campaign”. Young people, in turn, are expected to accept that distinction and challenge those whom the state places on the other side of it.

A method of training trolls?

Opposition figures and independent observers have long described such camps as a form of “troll factory”. Critics argue that their purpose is not to encourage independent thinking but to prepare young people to defend the official position on social media, in online discussions and before international audiences. They say that, under the banner of patriotism, organisers cultivate emotional attachment and ideological loyalty while encouraging participants to view critical voices as “hostile”.

Every country seeks to use its diaspora as a tool of soft power, and Azerbaijan is no exception. The problem, critics argue, is that the shrinking space for domestic criticism places a disproportionately heavy burden on young Azerbaijanis abroad to “defend” the official line. They must adapt to societies where freedom of expression is a fundamental principle while remaining loyal to Baku’s official narrative. For many young people, that contradiction can create genuine tension.

Muradov says, “We are open to dialogue”, while also insisting, “We will not tolerate black PR.” This raises an obvious question: what qualifies as “well-founded criticism”, and what counts as a “biased campaign”? If official media portray the questions and slogans heard on the streets of Berlin as a provocation, where is the line for young people who raise the same issues in international media or at academic forums?

World.title: We've never seen the Sun in this much detail before
World.content:
The Sun's surface is constantly churning with hot, glowing plasma.

Those swirling eddies play a huge role in the Sun's occasional violent outbursts, but they're difficult to see because it is so bright.

Now astronomers have used the world's largest solar telescope to capture the highest-resolution imagery ever taken of our star's roiling surface.

It shows a section of the Sun about 5,000 by 3,500 kilometres in size: a zone that, on Earth, could comfortably enclose mainland Australia.

Loading...

The stunning imagery also captures a never-before-seen physical process, which the researchers have described in the journal Nature.

Michael Wheatland, an astrophysicist at the University of Sydney who wasn't involved with the research, said the imagery was "just incredible".

"We've never observed the Sun at that resolution," Professor Wheatland said.

"In this amazing detail, we see all of this really interesting fundamental physics happening."

Whirling patterns on the Sun's surface

The observations show the solar surface, called the photosphere, constantly swirls and flows with plasma.

According to the researchers, these ebbs and flows show the plasma undergoes a physical process called Kelvin-Hemholtz instability.

This effect happens when different types of fluids mix, causing small fluctuations at the borders between them.

Loading...

"You see it in clouds, you see it in the ocean, you see it whenever you have fluids," Professor Wheatland said.

"But we haven't actually seen it on the Sun in a way that's really unambiguous. I think the evidence here is completely unambiguous."

On Earth, this instability is often driven by fluids of different temperatures or densities, or moving at different speeds. On the Sun, the differences come from changes in magnetism.

The striations seen on the solar surface are caused by differences in magnetism. (Supplied: NSF/NSO/AURA/MPS)

"When you mix the fluid, you move the magnetic field around as well," Professor Wheatland said.

This mixing can lead to an increase in energy which could be the reason the Sun's corona — the outer part of its atmosphere — is so hot.

The Sun's surface is roughly 5,500 degrees Celsius, but the corona above it can reach 2 million degrees.

The solar telescope in Hawaii

Hannah Schunker, an astrophysicist at the University of Newcastle, said because the Sun was so close to Earth — a mere 149 million kilometres away — it was the only place astronomers could study the surface of a star in detail.

"The Sun is like an astrophysical laboratory," Dr Schunker, who also wasn't involved with the new research, said.

The observations were made with the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope, in Hawaii, which is run by the US National Science Foundation.

The telescope is named after Daniel Inouye, who represented Hawaii in the US Senate from 1963 to his death in 2012. (Supplied: NSF/NSO/AURA)

Solar telescopes use the same basic technology as other large optical telescopes — large mirrors and lenses which magnify light — but since they're designed to focus on the Sun, they need to be purpose-built.

"The Sun is just so bright and produces so much more heat and light than a distant star," Dr Schunker said.

"So it requires specialised filters, cooling systems and instruments that can be safely pointed at the Sun without damaging the telescope."

Friedrich Woeger, senior scientist at the US National Solar Observatory and co-lead author on the paper, said that while preparing for and analysing the observations required months of work, the imagery they captured spans only a few minutes.

"The acquisition of the data used in the study itself actually did not take much longer than five minutes," Dr Woeger said.

Predicting space weather

Dr Schunker said was important to understand the Sun's magnetic field because it drives all space weather.

The science behind auroras and solar storms Behind every solar storm there is a sunspot, and some serious physics.

While these images only capture a small part of the Sun's surface for a small period of time, she said data and modelling like this could eventually be used to predict things like solar flares.

"These very small-scale changes that are happening on the surface of the Sun, they are responsible for all the larger scale things happening in the atmosphere, and we've never been able to see them before," Dr Schunker said.

Flares and other solar phenomena can cause bright auroras on Earth, and in serious cases prompt power outages and damage to satellites and other technology.

"We can take the small-scale physics and put it into the larger-scale models, and this will open the door to, hopefully, better weather predictions, better predictions of flares, [and] better predictions of how heat is transported up to the corona," Dr Schunker said.

Future observations with the Inouye telescope and other instruments will help to model the Sun's surface more closely. (Supplied: NSF/NSO/AURA/MPS)

Dr Woeger said it would be valuable to have observations of a larger section of the Sun's surface to get more data on the patterns they observed.

"We are planning for future Inouye Solar Telescope measurements with instruments that provide more information about velocities and magnetic field of the plasma on the Sun," Dr Woeger said.

Professor Wheatland said the imagery signified an exciting time for solar astronomy.

" Progress will be made in some of the big, outstanding questions in solar physics. "

World.title: Woman arrested after four men stabbed in central London
World.content:
A woman has been arrested after four people were stabbed in one of central London's busiest tourist hotspots on Wednesday.

Emergency services were called to Endell Street, Covent Garden, around 12:30pm local time (9:30pm AEST), and an air ambulance landed in Trafalgar Square as part of the response to the incident.

Police said four men, aged in their 30s, 40s and 50s, had sustained stab wounds. They are receiving treatment in hospital.

A 47-year-old woman has been arrested on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon and assault. She remains in custody.

Police say they believe the incident was mental health related.

"Officers seized a pair of scissors at the scene," a police statement read.

In a statement, the London Ambulance Service said: "We treated four patients at the scene and took them all to a major trauma centre as a priority by road."

The area is known for large crowds and is popular with tourists. (PA: James Manning via AP)

Covent Garden is renowned as among London's premier theatre and entertainment districts, and draws large crowds both day and night.

A large crowd of people could be seen watching the air ambulance take off from Trafalgar Square later in the day.

By 3:30pm local time police road blocks in the area had been removed.

Matt Bishop was in the area at the time and say police in a "stand off" with a woman.

"As the situation developed two police officers turned up one of which took the legs out from under her and pinned her down," he said.

"There was a man nearby who was having his back treated for a stab wound."

Mr Bishop said the woman police arrested had been "shouting incoherently" at the time.

"Police were asking what language she was speaking. Either she was speaking another language or just gibberish."

World.title: Exiled Bangladesh PM vows to return despite facing death sentence
World.content:
Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has vowed to return to her country despite being sentenced to death for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown against student protesters.

The 78-year-old fled to India in August 2024 by helicopter at the height of the student-led uprising that toppled her government.

She has remained there since despite Bangladesh authorities seeking her extradition.

On Wednesday evening, she delivered an audio message to mark the second anniversary of the uprising that ousted her.

How Bangladesh's 'Iron Lady' was toppled As she flew to neighbouring India, thousands of protesters stormed Sheikh Hasina's official residence, some lying on a bed, another munching on chicken leg pieces and others trying on her clothes.

She was due to make the address via videolink at an event hosted by the Foreign Correspondents' Club of South Asia in New Delhi alongside her son, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, and other speakers.

It would have been her first public appearance since she was forced to resign — but instead only an audio message was played.

In it, she said that the ban on her Awami League party should be lifted.

"I will return to my people," she said.

"They may try to implicate me with fabricated cases, but fear cannot decide my duty to the people, my life or beyond."

She said she would share the exact date of her return and other details when the time was right.

Protesters demanded Hasina step down during protests which began as a student movement against a government jobs quota. (AP: Rajib Dhar)

It was not immediately clear why she did not appear on video, unlike her party colleagues and her son, who spoke before her.

Bangladesh had warned the country's media not to publicise Hasina's statements, saying that doing so would violate a 2024 court order that prohibited the publishing or broadcasting of her speeches and statements.

India-Bangladesh relations strained since Hasina's ousting

The anti-government protests forced Hasina to resign after 20 years in power.

She was sentenced to death in 2025 for crimes against humanity over her crackdown on the demonstrations.

Bangladesh court issues death sentence against ex-PM who fled country A Bangladesh court has sentenced ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina to death after finding her guilty of crimes against humanity.

It was a verdict she dismissed as legally void.

Hasina's aide Abu Obaidha Arin said Dhaka's "efforts to silence dissent cannot extinguish voices" beyond the country's borders.

Bangladesh's State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said Bangladesh had repeatedly conveyed its concerns to India over Hasina and other Awami League leaders making political statements from Indian soil.

Indian foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the event was being organised by a private media entity and the Indian government had "no involvement whatsoever in it".

"Neither does it endorse any views that may be expressed at the forum," he said.

Relations between the neighbours have been strained since Hasina's ousting, though both sides have recently signalled a willingness to improve ties under Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's government, which took office after February's election.

Reuters

World.title: What the success of 'Michigan Mamdani' says about the future of the Democrats
World.content:
In what was a high-stakes primary day across five US states, the bitter Democratic Senate battle between Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens in Michigan drew the most attention.

But the Associated Press now projects Dr El-Sayed has ultimately won, a result that is expected to shape the Democrats' messaging to voters and how it challenges US President Donald Trump ahead of November's crucial midterms.

Dr El-Sayed, a progressive epidemiologist who is pushing to cut the influence of corporate money in politics and has criticised US aid to Israel, ran as an outsider, with the support of senator Bernie Sanders and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

His opponent, Haley Stevens, was a well-funded moderate, with the backing of establishment Democrat figures including Michigan's governor Gretchen Whitmer and senate minority leader Chuck Schumer.

The two candidates came to represent an ideological battle between the establishment and progressives within the Democrat Party, and the Michigan contest was dominated by their views on issues like US-Israel relations and the country's future.

"A year and a half ago, you wouldn't have thought there was any way that Zohran Mamdani could have won [the mayor's race] in New York," David Smith, associate professor at the United States Studies Center at the University of Michigan, told the ABC.

"But he ran quite an extraordinary campaign, and even though there was a lot of scepticism that a Muslim who branded himself as a socialist could win a general election, could win a Democratic primary even, he won.

"A lot of people saw El-Sayed as a test of whether something like that can happen outside of a major deep blue city like New York."

Michigan is one of the nation's key swing states, a genuinely purple region that has bounced between Democrats to Republicans and back again in presidential elections.

And what happened in the August 4 primary, both at the ballot box and in the immediate aftermath, will serve as a test case for Democrats in the lead-up to 2028.

Who is Abdul El-Sayed?

The son of Egyptian immigrants, Dr El-Sayed, 41, was born and raised in south-east Michigan.

He is the first Muslim to win a seat in the US Senate.

Abdul El-Sayed was an outsider in the Michigan primary race. (Reuters: Rebecca Cook)

He studied medicine at university but has spent most of his career working in public health policy, rather than as a practising physician.

He made universal healthcare central to his campaign, along with higher taxes for billionaires and reducing the amount of money pouring into US politics.

His platform and campaign style have drawn comparisons to New York City's democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani, although Dr El-Sayed does not describe himself as a socialist and has played down the similarities.

"I am who I am," he told Slate. "The comparisons are going to keep coming, I guess that's on you to make."

Dr El-Sayed has also called for the US to cut military aid to Israel, accusing the country of committing genocide in Gaza.

Michigan is home to the United States' highest proportion of Arab voters, and anger towards the Biden-Harris administration's handling of the conflict was considered a factor in Democrats losing the state in the 2024 presidential election.

Why has this race been so closely watched?

The Michigan race was a primary election, meaning candidates from the same party were battling each other to become their party's representative in a general poll.

Dr El-Sayed still needs to beat Republican Mike Rogers in November if he is going to enter the Senate.

Michigan is one of nation’s key swing states. (Reuters: Dieu-Nalio Chery)

But this first stage of the process has attracted nationwide attention because it highlights a broader divide over the future of the Democratic Party, two years after its bruising 2024 defeat.

Dr El-Sayed's opponent, Haley Stevens, is a 43-year-old moderate who is currently serving her fourth term in the House of Representatives.

Ms Stevens has criticised Dr El-Sayed as a "celebrity candidate", arguing he will not be able to win over enough swing voters to defeat Mr Rogers.

Unlike Mr Mamdani's New York, where voters predominantly support Democratic candidates, Michigan has swung between the two parties at the last four presidential polls.

"People are watching the midterms for control of the House and Senate, but also because they're sort of an indicator of what the party might be headed for in 2028," Emily Lawler, politics editor at the Detroit Free Press, told ABC Radio National.

"Especially in a swing state like Michigan… if a candidate like Abdul El-Sayed were to win the primary and then win the general, that could indicate a really different direction for the Democratic Party than we've seen in the last couple of decades."

Why is so much outside spending involved?

In the fierce battle between the two candidates, a record amount of money was invested in the Michigan primary.

Much of it came from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), a prominent lobby group that works with both parties to "strengthen America's relationship with Israel", and its affiliated groups.

They spent close to $US30 million ($42.5 million) backing Ms Stevens against Dr El-Sayed in what was believed to be their largest investment ever in a single race and a clear sign of just how high AIPAC considered the stakes of the primary to be.

Haley Stevens has been criticised by her oppontent over her donors. (Reuters: Robin Buckson/Pool)

"Both AIPAC and its opponents see these Democratic contests at the moment as a struggle over the future of the party. They both see it as not just one contest, this is actually a tipping point in terms of how the party goes," Dr Smith said.

" I would say in a nutshell, they see it as a struggle over the future of the party. "

The Gaza war has split the party over US backing of Israel and the issue has since become a lightning rod in Democratic politics.

Dr El-Sayed and his supporters, who relied on grassroots campaigning and digital donations to fundraise, ridiculed his opponent's funding throughout the campaign, accusing Ms Stevens of being an "employee of billionaires".

Ms Stevens outspent Dr El-Sayed on the airwaves by at least nine times, according to political ad tracker, AdImpact.

It found outside groups spent $US64 million ($90.6 million) for Stevens, while Dr El-Sayed had only about $US7 million ($9.9 million) spent for him by either his campaign or his allies.

When Ms Stevens was asked whether she welcomed the money flowing to her campaign coffers from AIPAC by the Associated Press, she responded: "Anyone who supported me is supporting me because of my dedication to the people of Michigan, and the things that I have done for Michiganders."

What other races are happening?

Voters in Kansas, Missouri, Virginia and Washington were also picking nominees for the US Senate and the US House on August 4.

A few of those races included competitive swing districts in Virginia that were set to help decide control of the chamber in November.

Voting in Virginia came after the state's supreme court overturned a referendum to redraw its House map to create four new winnable seats for the Democrats.

What could Michigan tell us about the midterms?

The fallout from the Michigan primary race will likely stretch far beyond the result, and all the way to the contest in November.

With the state swinging wildly between the two parties, a win there is seen as necessary for Democrats if they have any hope of winning a Senate majority later this year.

"Dr El-Sayed could be a signal that people are looking for candidates who are demanding very serious change," Dr Smith said.

But he said anti-Trump sentiment could ultimately be the biggest factor in how people vote in November.

Who's proud to be American? Donald Trump has been pushing a patriotic message ahead of a July 4 milestone, but some Americans say they feel no national pride at this point in their country's history.

"Because with President Trump's approval rating so low and with people's perceptions of the economy being so bad because of the very real cost-of-living pressures that everybody is facing, it might not even matter who Democratic candidates are in that environment," Dr Smith said.

"People could just be in a mood to throw out Republicans."

Polls so far do not indicate the Republicans are in that much danger yet. But Dr Smith warned that in three more months, the situation could be very different.

"The economy could still get worse. The war in Iran could get worse. President Trump's approval ratings could get worse. And under those circumstances, it might not even matter who the Democratic candidate is."

World.title: At least 17 dead in Kyiv as Zelenskyy calls for more air defences
World.content:
Russian missile and drone strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region killed 17 people and injured 44 others, smashing business premises and a train station, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

The targets hit included a brewing company, a warehouse for construction material, and a mail sorting office that had nothing to do with the war, Mr Zelenskyy said.

But the Russian Defence Ministry said the businesses masked ties to the military.

The Tuesday night attack, lasting about two hours, was the latest in a series of large-scale Russian ballistic missile strikes that have become near-routine this summer.

Zelenskyy shares video of Russian drone on 'safari' Ukraine accuses Russia of committing a war crime after video is released showing a drone chasing down and wounding a vegetable seller in the southern city of Kherson.

Moscow is exploiting Ukraine's critical shortage of interceptor missiles for the US-made Patriot systems, the sole air defence weapon in its arsenal able to shoot down ballistic missiles.

Mr Zelenskyy has pleaded with other countries to send more of the ammunition made scarcer by the Iran war.

Supplies of air defense missiles to Ukraine during the first half of this year tumbled to one-third of the 2025 level, Mr Zelenskyy said.

"Ballistic interceptors are what could have saved the lives of those killed today," Mr Zelenskyy said on social media.

"It is very important for our partners to understand that delays in supplying them, or a reluctance to hand over anti-ballistic systems, lead directly to such horrific casualties and destruction."

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has again implored for more ballistic interceptors. (Reuters: Stringer)

Russia says it struck war-related targets in Kyiv region

Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Mr Zelenskyy, said the war of attrition is entering a new phase.

"The enemy is attacking everything indiscriminately — retail warehouses, food storage facilities, logistics hubs, enterprises, building materials warehouses," he said on Facebook.

Mykhailo Hukov, a 40-year-old Kyiv warehouse worker, said an air raid warning that included a ballistic missile threat sounded just after Tuesday midnight, prompting an immediate evacuation order.

"So everyone started running," he told The Associated Press.

"I turned everyone around so they wouldn't go back inside for their backpacks."

How a Sydney band became massive in wartime Ukraine Sydney band breathe. managed to become the only international act at Kyiv's Atlas music festival. What they saw is etched in their collective memories.

Minutes later, in an underground shelter, they heard "some very loud, very loud explosions."

Ukraine's largest private postal operator, Nova Poshta, said a Russian cluster munition destroyed one of its sorting centres in Kyiv.

The Russian Defence Ministry said the centre was "storing and distributing dual-use goods, including those used in the production of long-and-medium-range uncrewed aerial vehicles, as well as robotic systems and electronic warfare systems."

It claimed that two other logistics centres in the Kyiv region stored drones or components for drones.

Separately, the Russian ministry said its forces hit three bulk carriers on the Black Sea south of Odesa that it claimed were transporting weapons and military equipment for the Ukrainian armed forces.

Ukrainian officials did not comment on that claim.

Ukraine's largest private postal operator, Nova Poshta had a sorting centre destroyed. (AP: Efrem Lukatsky)

Truck drivers make a narrow escape

Ivan Braga, a 46-year-old truck driver from Moldova who was in Kyiv during the attack, said he and a colleague ran from their vehicle when it was struck by shrapnel in a blast wave.

"We didn't even have time to grab our documents or anything else," Mr Braga told AP.

"I couldn't believe it. I'd already been in Kyiv and had heard explosions before, but nothing like today."

One of the companies that came under heavy fire was Epicentr, one of Ukraine's largest retail and construction chains.

It said in a statement on Facebook that "in minutes, Russian missiles destroyed what the company had built over decades".

One employee was killed and three others were injured.

According to the Russian Defence Ministry, the Epicentr logistics centre handled order processing, sorting, storing, and delivery of dual-use goods and components for drone production.

Five were killed and 19 injured in the central Moscow event on August 2. (AP: Pavel Bednyakov)

Russian drone supplier injured in car explosion

Meanwhile in Russia, the director of a factory supplying drones to the Russian military was badly injured when his car exploded, according to reports on Wednesday, local time.

The state TASS and RIA Novosti agencies said Vladimir Tkachuk was hospitalised in grave condition following the explosion late Tuesday in Bolshoy Istok just outside Yekaterinburg, 1,400 kilometres east of Moscow.

It did not immediately give details of the explosion or say who could be responsible.

There was no immediate comment from the authorities.

Mr Tkachuk headed the Uraldronzavod factory that manufactures Upyr (Russian for Ghoul) drones.

Drones make life in Russia's cities a 'nightmare' For years, people in Russia's largest and most affluent cities were shielded from the impacts of their country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but not anymore.

Mr Tkachuk, a small-scale entrepreneur, set up a team of engineers that developed the Upyr and organised its production near Yekaterinburg, Russia's fourth-largest city and a key industrial hub in the Ural Mountains

The Upyr, a cheap and simple first-person view drone, was hailed by troops for the protection it offers against jamming.

Russian authorities have blamed Kyiv for a series of bombings and other attacks against senior military officials after Moscow sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022.

The explosion followed Saturday's deadly bombing at a Moscow restaurant, which the Russian Embassy in Rome blamed on Ukraine, describing it as an attempt to intimidate the Italian community in Russia.

It said in a statement on Monday, lcoal time, that the attack on the Balzi Rossi restaurant killed five and injured 19.

AP

World.title: Artists from remote Australia among winners at prestigious fashion awards
World.content:
A unique partnership between a remote Northern Territory women's centre and an art studio in India has beeen recognised at this year's prestigious National Indigenous Fashion Awards (NIFA).

The event is Australia's largest annual showcase of First Nations fashion and celebrates the best Indigenous designers, artists and creatives from across the country.

This year's National Indigenous Fashion Awards were presented at Darwin's Deckchair Cinema. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

This year's ceremony took place in Darwin on Larrakia country, and was attended by locals and art enthusiasts from all over.

Presented by the Darwin Aboriginal Art Fair Foundation as part of Indigenous Fashion Projects, the event follows last week's sold-out Country to Couture runway celebration.

Cindy Rostron is pictured at Tharangini Studio, holding one of the wooden stamps used by the designers and modelling clothes crafted by her mother and aunty. (Supplied: Ziian Carey)

International collaboration recognised

A partnership between the Bábbarra Women's Centre, in the remote community of Maningrida, and India's Tharangini Studio won NIFA's Community Collaboration award — a category that recognises strong, two-way relationships between First Nations communities and the textile and fashion industry.

Padmini Govind travelled from India to accept tonight's award alongside Janet Marawarr, who represented Bábbarra Women's Centre.

The collaboration between Bábbarra Women's Centre and Tharangini Studio won an award at this year's event. (Supplied: Anahita Ananth)

Their collaboration translated 78 Indigenous designs from 14 clans into woodblock stamps used for printing, sharing the ancient techniques that have been passed down over hundreds of years in Bangalore, also known as Bengaluru.

Travelling overseas to collaborate and then keeping in touch online, the two women-led organisations found what Govind described as "textile magic".

Loading...

"It's a craft-led dialogue because, when they visited us, English is our fourth language and English is also a third language for them," she said.

" But we felt we really didn't need a common spoken language to create all this textile magic. "

Govind said the lino printing tools used by Bábbarra artists tended to disintegrate over time, but woodblocks could last up to 100 years if they were made from the right materials.

Deborah Wurrkidj (left) and Rosanna Bonson wearing sari designs that were printed by hand at Tharangini Studio. (Supplied: Ziian Carey/Anahita Ananth)

"In way, it's preserving stories of artists who are here and also who are no longer with us," she said.

"We really feel blessed to be part of their cultural legacy."

Padmini Govind and Janet Marawarr say the artistic practice helps pass on generations of cultural knowledge. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Govind said the art was about more than design.

"It's a piece of their family history that's been entrusted to us," she said.

Marawarr said the partnership would help First Nations clans pass that important cultural knowledge down to the next generation.

"[We can] teach our children for the future and [show] the old people, to see how they print the design," she said.

Abigail Namundja holding the wooden stamp her late mother, J Wurrkidj, designed at the Bábbarra Women's Centre. (Supplied: Ziian Carey)

Family history, culture highlighted

NIFA's major Indigenous Fashion Designer award went to Delvene Cockatoo-Collins, from Quandamooka Country in south-east Queensland, who said she was "overwhelmed" by the win.

Her work features sustainably-sourced, handmade textiles including clothing, accessories and homewares.

"My work always starts with a story and I'm wearing what I make — that is hand-printed, naturally dyed, small batch, all connected to my mum and her stories, my grandmother's written and oral history," Cockatoo-Collins said.

Delvene Cockatoo-Collins says her works are connected to family stories, passed down over generations. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

She described the annual event as crucial in connecting artists from remote corners of the country, supporting them to share stories and knowledge.

"[Fashion] a visual way of sharing a story, and it can be read almost instantly on the runway," the designer said.

"When people look at that work, they can see that it's from the island that belongs to our family line: my granny's granny."

Natural Tiwi Islands materials used in art

Michelle Pulatuwayu Woody Minnapinni, from the remote community of Milikapiti on the Tiwi Islands, took out the Traditional Adornment award for the unique baskets, armbands and headwear she crafted by hand.

The handmade bark basket, known on Tiwi Islands as a "tunga", is used to carry objects such as food. (Supplied)

This category, which encourages the creation of traditional regalia, recognises designs that are made and worn to express culture.

Minnapinni said her work was crafted using materials of cultural significance to Tiwi people, including pandanus leaves and bird feathers.

She learned her skills from an older sister, who has now passed away, so the art prize is especially significant.

Michelle Pulatuwayu Woody Minnapinni crafted the wearable art, or "parmijini", by hand. (Supplied)

Minnapinni said she hoped to share those skills with her younger family members.

"It's been a long journey to make it this far," she said.

"I'm really proud of myself, but also I had to do this to honour my old people, and my late sister, and just pass down the traditional knowledge."

The handmade designs were crafted with natural materials, including bark. (Supplied)
