World.title: WA's NAPLAN results trigger 'concern' for year 3s
World.content:
Western Australia's NAPLAN results show 40 per cent of year 3 students are struggling with numeracy, but year 9 students are out-performing the national average in every category this year.

Figures also show year 3 and 5 students ranked below the average NAPLAN score for every category. Year 7 students ranked below average for every category apart from spelling, in which students achieved a mark of 543.1, compared to the national average of 541.6.

WA's year 9 students were the state's best performers.

Despite the younger years largely experiencing below-average scores, there were some improvements on last year's figures.

Year 5 grammar and punctuation saw a score increase of 0.8 per cent compared to last year, and year 7 numeracy was up 0.7 per cent.

The largest drop, however, was recorded in year 3 writing, which was down 1.7 per cent compared to last year.

Roughly 1.2 million students across Australia participated in NAPLAN testing this year and were assessed in five categories — writing, spelling, reading, numeracy, and grammar and punctuation.

When looking at how students ranked across the four score categories — "needs additional support", "developing", "strong" and "exceeding" — from lowest to highest, the stand-out figure from WA was year 3 numeracy scores, which saw 39.9 per cent of those students place in the bottom two tiers.

System 'working well'

WA Education Minister Sabine Winton said the NAPLAN figures were "encouraging" for the year 9 cohort.

"For me, the real value in whether we are actually having great outcomes in our educational system is the growth that you bring to each and every child, whether it's from term to term, from year to year," she said.

"It is clear our education system is working well to add to that growth, and it's working particularly well when you consider our year 9 results.

" No matter where the starting point is, our schools must be doing something fantastic over a number of years to get our year 9s into that strong position. "

Sabine Winton was buoyed by the state's year 9 results. (ABC News: Kenith Png)

But Ms Winton acknowledged that the year 3 numeracy scores were of "most concern" in WA and across the nation.

"It really does, I think, reflect what I hear anecdotally from my mates in terms of more children with development delays, the more complex needs coming into our school system," she said.

Opposition education spokesperson Liam Staltari shared Ms Winton's concern over the year 3 scores and said the "warning signs" should not be be ignored.

Liam Staltari says the government needs to do more to help students who are struggling. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"If I were the parent of an eight- or a nine-year-old, I would be concerned, because if we don't support our kids in those critical early years, we know that they fall behind later in schooling," he said.

Mr Staltari said the government needed to do more to set up children for success in year 3, pointing to low student-to-teacher ratios in WA classrooms and teacher burnout.

World.title: Murder accused to remain in custody as lawyers struggle to find suitable bail location
World.content:
Fierce opposition, community riots and an unmanned police station are among the issues that have left a 20-year-old man charged with murder in custody for months while he waits for lawyers to find a suitable location for bail.

Justin Bukulatjpi was charged with murdering a man and unlawfully causing serious harm to another person during a brawl in Milingimbi in April.

In May, the Northern Territory Supreme Court granted Mr Bukulatjpi bail to live with family on the Tiwi Islands — a decision that was strongly opposed by Crown prosecutor Deborah Mandie, who said the prosecution had a "very strong" case against him.

Ms Mandie told the court prosecutors would rely on more than 10 minutes of mobile phone footage of the incident, in which she said the accused could be seen wielding a knife above his head before the other man fell to the ground.

Despite that, Justice Judith Kelly said she had a "high degree of confidence" Mr Bukulatjpi would follow his bail conditions.

However, days before he was due to be released, traditional owners wrote to the NT police commissioner expressing concerns his presence would bring further unrest to the area, preventing his release.

A week later, there were riots in the community and the Tiwi Islands' executive director of township leasing blocked him from entering public spaces — actions that Justice Kelly described as "unacceptable".

Justin Bukulatjpi's planned bail to the Tiwi Islands was blocked by community riots involving at least 100 residents. (Supplied: Rebecca Parker)

Mr Bukulatjpi has faced court several times since his first appearance more than two months ago.

However, each of his proposed bail addresses have so far been found to be unsuitable, leaving him on remand as lawyers continue searching for an alternative.

Judge requests undertaking to the court

On Wednesday, defence barrister Louise Dart proposed her client live with family on Warruwi, a tiny Indigenous community on the isolated South Goulburn Island, 290 kilometres north-east of Darwin.

But the case was delayed again after Ms Mandie told the court the Warruwi police station was unmanned for five weeks at a time, effectively ruling out electronic monitoring, and argued that Mr Bukulatjpi remained a flight risk.

Ms Dart argued her client had strong family ties in the community and would have little opportunity to flee.

"It's a question of where would he go? He's a person of limited means, limited English … I don't think he's going to flee the jurisdiction," she said.

Judith Kelly says breaching an undertaking could be ruled contempt of court. (Supplied: Supreme Court of the Northern Territory)

Justice Kelly requested Ms Dart make enquiries as to whether any "men in authority, who may be able to exert more influence, on Mr Bukulatjpi" would be willing to provide an undertaking to the court to "use their best endeavours" to make sure he remained at the bail address.

She said a breach of such an undertaking could result in a charge of contempt of court.

"[If a] respected male [or] elder from the community is willing to put their reputation on the line … then it seems to me that that would probably overcome the sorts of concerns raised by Ms Mandie," she said.

The case has been adjourned until September and Mr Bukulatjpi was remanded in custody.

World.title: El-Sayed wins in Michigan as Democrats veer left in crucial midterms contest
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaUS politics El-Sayed wins in Michigan as Democrats veer left in crucial midterms contest Michael Koziol August 6, 2026 — 12:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Democrats in the midwestern state of Michigan have chosen Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing Muslim doctor, to be their candidate for the US Senate in a result with seismic consequences for the midterm elections and US politics. They rejected Haley Stevens, a four-term Democratic congresswoman heavily backed by the party establishment, despite outside groups spending more than $US60 million ($84.5 million) for her in the most expensive Democratic Senate primary ever. Progressive stars Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Bernie Sanders campaigning for Abdul El-Sayed in July. Bloomberg His victory comes at a time when Republicans led by US President Donald Trump are painting Democrats nationwide as being overtaken by communists who want to destroy America, end capitalism and adopt a range of policies that sit outside the mainstream. El-Sayed, who was backed by progressive hero Bernie Sanders and democratic socialist Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, will be the Democratic candidate for a seat which the party must hold if they are to win control of the Senate in November.



The 41-year-old campaigned on a platform of taking private finance out of politics, putting money in the pockets of regular Michiganders, and universal healthcare. He promised higher taxes on the wealthy, and ending US military aid and arms sales to Israel. The contest was tighter than many recent polls predicted, with El-Sayed winning 48.5 per cent to 47.5, or about 15,000 votes. CNN and the Associated Press called the race for him just before 10am on Wednesday (midnight AEST), when 99 per cent of the counting was complete. Abdul El-Sayed at an election night party on Tuesday while the results were still too close to call. Bloomberg Speaking at 1am local time when the votes were still being tallied, both candidates said it was time to put the bruising contest behind them come together. “There is so much more that unites us than divides us,” El-Sayed told his supporters. “Tomorrow we begin to mend fences.”



Michigan, a swing state that voted for Trump in 2016 and 2024, last sent a Republican to the US Senate in the 1990s. But Mike Rogers, the Republican whom El-Sayed will take on in November, narrowly lost last time. Most experts say El Sayed’s victory will make it harder for Democrats to hold the seat, while strategists were soul-searching about the party’s direction, and whether it was moving too far to the left. The support of the Democratic establishment and a significant funding advantage was not enough to secure victory for Haley Stevens. Bloomberg Adrian Hemond, chief executive of Grassroots Midwest, a bipartisan Michigan-based public affairs group, told this masthead last week: “If he wins the primary and then loses the general election in the fall, it’s disastrous for national progressives.” El-Sayed is the first Muslim to win the Democratic nomination for the US Senate (though not the first Republican), and would be the first Muslim to enter the US Senate if he wins in November.



Unlike Ocasio-Cortez or Zohran Mamdani in New York, he is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. But he has attended their events in the past, and the DSA supported his campaign. “His policy platform is socialist,” Hemond said. El Sayed’s victory represents a heavy defeat for the Democratic elite. Stevens had endorsements from Michigan’s Democratic governor Gretchen Whitmer, multiple senators and representatives, mayors and former officeholders. There were no results on Tuesday night with the race closer than most polls predicted. Bloomberg Sanders, appearing on CNN as the votes were still counted, said he couldn’t recall anything like it. “Abdul El-Sayed is taking on the entire Michigan Democratic establishment,” Sanders said. “He’s taking on the entire national Democratic establishment. He has been outspent 10 to one.”



Related Article US election Can a left-wing Muslim win the Midwest? Or are Democrats about to make a big mistake The $US60 million in outside funding supporting Stevens’ campaign included more than $US30 million from pro-Israel lobby groups, which became an important focus of the campaign. Polls show the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which funds pro-Israel candidates via super PACs, is a toxic entity among Democrats, especially younger ones - as is support for Israel more broadly. Stevens remained a staunch supporter of the Jewish state, and once told a Hanukkah event: “Israel comes to me in my dreams.” El-Sayed ended up comfortably winning Kent County, which takes in the city of Grand Rapids. He also easily won the state capital, Lansing, and Ann Arbor, home to the University of Michigan.



Related Article Explainer

US election ‘A referendum on the president’: How do the midterms work? Stevens won Detroit, largely thanks to its majority population of African Americans, who are less likely to support left-wing candidates than white Democrats. Trump weighed in on Tuesday morning claiming, without evidence, that Wayne Country - which takes in Detroit - was one of the most corrupt voting areas in the US. “Great news for the Republican Party,” he said. “El-Sayed, a communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner … Now, the Dumocrats crazy policies will only get worse!” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Not just upheaval: AI could deliver $120b boost and more jobs
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAI Not just upheaval: AI could deliver $120b boost and more jobs Shane Wright August 6, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Artificial intelligence could deliver the national economy a desperately needed productivity boost worth almost $120 billion and support the creation of tens of thousands of jobs, a nation-leading analysis has found. Compiled by consultancy EY, the modelling of AI’s impact on the ability of workers to boost output suggests the technology will increase the size of the economy by between 2.6 per cent and 3.2 per cent by the middle of the next decade. Data centres and the AI they support could deliver a much-needed boost to Australian productivity. Peter Rae That lift, worth between $95 billion and $116 billion, will contribute to an increase in jobs of between 36,000 and 44,000. The increase in productivity with AI is expected to generate an additional burst of business investment worth up to $38 billion. The country is in the midst of a data centre building boom, centred on NSW and Victoria, that by some comparisons will exceed the early 2010s mining boom that supercharged the economies of Western Australia and Queensland.



Related Article Exclusive

AI AI job disruption poised to upend Labor’s electoral map One Nation-style EY regional chief economist Cherelle Murphy said the research showed AI could turn around the nation’s poor productivity performance that many analysts believe has contributed to the sharp slowdown in Australians’ living standards and real wage growth. “The analysis shows that if AI-driven productivity gains flow through to investment, capacity and output, they could deliver a meaningful lift to economic growth,” she said. “The jobs story is not one of AI simply replacing workers across the economy. The modelling shows employment demand shifting towards sectors that benefit from stronger investment and household spending, while capital-intensive industries need fewer workers.” Critics of AI fear that in many cases the technology will wipe out jobs. There is limited evidence of that occurring in Australia to date.



Global human resources and payroll consultancy ADP on Wednesday released research suggesting only a quarter of all Australian workers believe their job is safe from elimination by AI, automation and changing demographics. But EY’s analysis shows many parts of the economy will need more staff because of AI. EY chief economist Cherelle Murphy says not only will AI lift productivity, it will create more jobs. Alex Ellinghausen Of the expected increase in jobs, close to 10,000 are forecast to be in construction, with a similar number in retail and wholesale trade. Another 6000 are expected to be created in the transport, postal and warehousing sector. Financial services, hospitality, arts and recreation services, real estate and manufacturing are all tipped to enjoy an increase in jobs due to AI.



The research shows the construction sector is boosted because of the need to build data centres while installing equipment in those businesses that increase their use of AI-related technology. Oxford Economics estimates the value of data centre construction and fit-outs alone will climb from $1 billion in 2020 to $26 billion this year to $60 billion in 2030. Other sectors would enjoy a lift in jobs as the productivity gains delivered by the technology lifts real wages, which is expected to boost spending on goods and services. But both the agriculture and broad mining sectors are forecast to suffer job losses of almost 3000 each. These two sectors are capital-intensive, making them more susceptible to greater automation that would enable a reduction in workers and reduce cost overheads.



Related Article Opinion

AI Did AI really ‘go rogue’? Not exactly, but we have plenty to fear Toby Walsh Chief scientist, AI Institute, UNSW Murphy noted workforce mobility and “targeted reskilling” would be needed if businesses were to fully benefit from AI. “A key priority for employers and government should be helping workers move into the sectors and parts of businesses where demand is expected to grow,” she said. EY’s research, however, did find the surge in AI-related construction could add to inflation pressures across the economy as it had in the United States. But that would be offset by the deflationary impact of higher productivity once the technology was in place. It also found AI could lead to more rapid retail price changes.



”AI may also increase risks around price stability, giving businesses the ability to continuously monitor demand, input costs and competitor prices,” it found. “This could increase the frequency of price changes and the spread of price shocks.” Most economic and political focus has been on the tens of billions of dollars being spent on the construction of data centres. But EY noted there had also been a substantial increase in AI-related software, apps and cloud platforms, with growth running at 8.3 per cent over the past 12 months. Software investment had also contributed to a sharp 4.9 per cent annual lift in research and development, well above the 0.6 per cent annual average increase through the 2010s. World.title: ‘Space for growth’: $55m cash splash to boost Brisbane primary schools’ capacity
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandSchools ‘Space for growth’: $55m cash splash to boost Brisbane primary schools’ capacity Catherine Strohfeldt August 5, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A $55 million cash splash will boost enrolment capacity for primary schools in Brisbane’s west by up to 450 places and enable schools to ditch their demountables. However, the area’s high school was not so lucky. On Wednesday, students and staff gathered to officially open Indooroopilly State School’s newest 12-classroom complex, while Toowong State School was expecting 11 additional classrooms in early 2027. Toowong State School students (left to right) Elliot Hodges, Felix Christian, Vera Williams, and Annie Xiang. Catherine Strohfeldt The new Toowong build would boost enrolments by 200 and include technology for its hard-of-hearing and deaf students, who comprise about one-third of enrolments. Year 5 student Elliot Hodges said “every day [the school] has a new student”, while his year 4 classmate, Vera Williams, said she was keen to see the campus grow alongside enrolments.



Indooroopilly State School principal Debbie Spanner. Facebook / John-Paul Langbroek “Overall, I really like the idea of the building because I’ve had experience in an older and more modern classrooms, and I think it would be nice for some of the other students to get that benefit,” she said. Principal Brendon Madden said the school was continuing to grow, with enrolments jumping by 29 students since the start of the year. He said the expansion, costing more than $20 million, would provide some breathing room. It also meant the school could remove three demountable buildings from its oval. “That will actually expand our play spaces for all our students … green space is really critical, they love to run around,” Madden said.



Indooroopilly State School principal Debbie Spanner said the school community was delighted with the new $34.1 million complex, which she said had enabled the school to get rid of four demountable classrooms. “We’ve got space for growth,” she said. The new building at Toowong State School was expected in early 2027. Catherine Strohfeldt “As a community, we feel a lot more confident to be able to cater for ... the children who are in our local community and want to come to Indooroopilly State School – we can meet that need.” While the Education Department and school were yet to hash out the exact details, the building – which included specialty music and staffroom spaces – was estimated to boost enrolments by about 250.





The three local primary campuses – Toowong, Indooroopilly, and Ironside state schools – enrolled a total of 2560 students in February this year. The campus expansions bring that number above 3000. While a new primary school had been earmarked for the area more than five years ago, the designs were scrapped in 2023 and the department de-prioritised the project. World.title: Leading man gets bossed in translation
World.content:
Tim Ingall of Scottsdale, Arizona (USA), is yet another viewer thwarted by the language barrier (C8): “While in Singapore on business, the hotel TV had limited channels, one of which was a local one, running a Malaysian soap opera. Closed captioning in English was provided but not in real time. For about 30 seconds a woman unleashed a verbal tirade against the offending male. No translation appeared as the tirade unfolded but when she stopped to draw breath, the closed caption ‘She is angry with him’ appeared. It was a case of ‘No shit, Sherlock’ on my part. I suspect the station’s budget could only cover ‘synopsis closed captioning’.”

Bryce Templeton of Mudgeeraba (Qld) went to see Paint Your Wagon in Italy: “As expected, it was dubbed into Italian, but I did not expect them to cut out all the songs! This kinda took the edge off it. After all, it is a musical.” Then again, Bryce, you might have dodged a bullet in avoiding Clint Eastwood belting out I Talk to the Trees.

“As an exchange school student to West Germany in 1972, my German exchange family delighted in showing me on TV that Skippy could speak German,” recalls Margaret Collins of Terrigal. “I have to say, I was surprised, too!” Was ist los, Skip?

“Nothing has cracked me up as much as hearing Hoges in fluent German in Ein Krokodil zum Kussen, sitting among a local Basel audience that did not laugh a lot,” says Frederika Steen of Chapel Hill (Qld).

Recent mentions of monotremes (C8) has Chris McKimm of Karangi in a flap: “Some years ago, on her morning walk, my wife noticed some agitation in the creek she was crossing. Closer inspection revealed we had a platypus in the stream that is the boundary of the back of our place. As recently as last week she saw ‘Polly’ swimming in the stream. It is an absolute privilege to have a monotreme in our stream.”

The modelling shows employment demand shifting towards sectors that benefit from stronger investment and household spending, while capital-intensive industries need fewer workers.” Critics of AI fear that in many cases the technology will wipe out jobs. There is limited evidence of that occurring in Australia to date.



Global human resources and payroll consultancy ADP on Wednesday released research suggesting only a quarter of all Australian workers believe their job is safe from elimination by AI, automation and changing demographics. But EY’s analysis shows many parts of the economy will need more staff because of AI. EY chief economist Cherelle Murphy says not only will AI lift productivity, it will create more jobs. Alex Ellinghausen Of the expected increase in jobs, close to 10,000 are forecast to be in construction, with a similar number in retail and wholesale trade. Another 6000 are expected to be created in the transport, postal and warehousing sector. Financial services, hospitality, arts and recreation services, real estate and manufacturing are all tipped to enjoy an increase in jobs due to AI.



The research shows the construction sector is boosted because of the need to build data centres while installing equipment in those businesses that increase their use of AI-related technology. Oxford Economics estimates the value of data centre construction and fit-outs alone will climb from $1 billion in 2020 to $26 billion this year to $60 billion in 2030. Other sectors would enjoy a lift in jobs as the productivity gains delivered by the technology lifts real wages, which is expected to boost spending on goods and services. But both the agriculture and broad mining sectors are forecast to suffer job losses of almost 3000 each. These two sectors are capital-intensive, making them more susceptible to greater automation that would enable a reduction in workers and reduce cost overheads.



Related Article Opinion

AI Did AI really ‘go rogue’? Not exactly, but we have plenty to fear Toby Walsh Chief scientist, AI Institute, UNSW Murphy noted workforce mobility and “targeted reskilling” would be needed if businesses were to fully benefit from AI. “A key priority for employers and government should be helping workers move into the sectors and parts of businesses where demand is expected to grow,” she said. EY’s research, however, did find the surge in AI-related construction could add to inflation pressures across the economy as it had in the United States. But that would be offset by the deflationary impact of higher productivity once the technology was in place. It also found AI could lead to more rapid retail price changes.



”AI may also increase risks around price stability, giving businesses the ability to continuously monitor demand, input costs and competitor prices,” it found. “This could increase the frequency of price changes and the spread of price shocks.” Most economic and political focus has been on the tens of billions of dollars being spent on the construction of data centres. But EY noted there had also been a substantial increase in AI-related software, apps and cloud platforms, with growth running at 8.3 per cent over the past 12 months. Software investment had also contributed to a sharp 4.9 per cent annual lift in research and development, well above the 0.6 per cent annual average increase through the 2010s. World.title: ‘Space for growth’: $55m cash splash to boost Brisbane primary schools’ capacity
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandSchools ‘Space for growth’: $55m cash splash to boost Brisbane primary schools’ capacity Catherine Strohfeldt August 5, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A $55 million cash splash will boost enrolment capacity for primary schools in Brisbane’s west by up to 450 places and enable schools to ditch their demountables. However, the area’s high school was not so lucky. On Wednesday, students and staff gathered to officially open Indooroopilly State School’s newest 12-classroom complex, while Toowong State School was expecting 11 additional classrooms in early 2027. Toowong State School students (left to right) Elliot Hodges, Felix Christian, Vera Williams, and Annie Xiang. Catherine Strohfeldt The new Toowong build would boost enrolments by 200 and include technology for its hard-of-hearing and deaf students, who comprise about one-third of enrolments. Year 5 student Elliot Hodges said “every day [the school] has a new student”, while his year 4 classmate, Vera Williams, said she was keen to see the campus grow alongside enrolments.



Indooroopilly State School principal Debbie Spanner. Facebook / John-Paul Langbroek “Overall, I really like the idea of the building because I’ve had experience in an older and more modern classrooms, and I think it would be nice for some of the other students to get that benefit,” she said. Principal Brendon Madden said the school was continuing to grow, with enrolments jumping by 29 students since the start of the year. He said the expansion, costing more than $20 million, would provide some breathing room. It also meant the school could remove three demountable buildings from its oval. “That will actually expand our play spaces for all our students … green space is really critical, they love to run around,” Madden said.



Indooroopilly State School principal Debbie Spanner said the school community was delighted with the new $34.1 million complex, which she said had enabled the school to get rid of four demountable classrooms. “We’ve got space for growth,” she said. The new building at Toowong State School was expected in early 2027. Catherine Strohfeldt “As a community, we feel a lot more confident to be able to cater for ... the children who are in our local community and want to come to Indooroopilly State School – we can meet that need.” While the Education Department and school were yet to hash out the exact details, the building – which included specialty music and staffroom spaces – was estimated to boost enrolments by about 250.





The three local primary campuses – Toowong, Indooroopilly, and Ironside state schools – enrolled a total of 2560 students in February this year. The campus expansions bring that number above 3000. While a new primary school had been earmarked for the area more than five years ago, the designs were scrapped in 2023 and the department de-prioritised the project. World.title: Leading man gets bossed in translation
World.content:
Tim Ingall of Scottsdale, Arizona (USA), is yet another viewer thwarted by the language barrier (C8): “While in Singapore on business, the hotel TV had limited channels, one of which was a local one, running a Malaysian soap opera. Closed captioning in English was provided but not in real time. For about 30 seconds a woman unleashed a verbal tirade against the offending male. No translation appeared as the tirade unfolded but when she stopped to draw breath, the closed caption ‘She is angry with him’ appeared. It was a case of ‘No shit, Sherlock’ on my part. I suspect the station’s budget could only cover ‘synopsis closed captioning’.”

Bryce Templeton of Mudgeeraba (Qld) went to see Paint Your Wagon in Italy: “As expected, it was dubbed into Italian, but I did not expect them to cut out all the songs! This kinda took the edge off it. After all, it is a musical.” Then again, Bryce, you might have dodged a bullet in avoiding Clint Eastwood belting out I Talk to the Trees.

“As an exchange school student to West Germany in 1972, my German exchange family delighted in showing me on TV that Skippy could speak German,” recalls Margaret Collins of Terrigal. “I have to say, I was surprised, too!” Was ist los, Skip?

“Nothing has cracked me up as much as hearing Hoges in fluent German in Ein Krokodil zum Kussen, sitting among a local Basel audience that did not laugh a lot,” says Frederika Steen of Chapel Hill (Qld).

Recent mentions of monotremes (C8) has Chris McKimm of Karangi in a flap: “Some years ago, on her morning walk, my wife noticed some agitation in the creek she was crossing. Closer inspection revealed we had a platypus in the stream that is the boundary of the back of our place. As recently as last week she saw ‘Polly’ swimming in the stream. It is an absolute privilege to have a monotreme in our stream.”
